Machine Learning.title: Density-Matrix Reinforcement Learning
Machine Learning.summary: What information does a reinforcement learning policy omit? At each state, a standard policy stores one probability per action. It has no place to record how actions relate to each other, such as which pairs go together and which conflict. We ask when this missing structure matters, and we give exact answers. We store the policy at each state as a density matrix, a positive semidefinite, unit-trace matrix borrowed from quantum information theory. We use it here as a purely classical data structure, computed on ordinary classical hardware. The diagonal holds the usual action probabilities. The off-diagonal entries, called coherences, are new parameters. This gives density-matrix reinforcement learning (DMRL). Coherences change outcomes in two settings. First, suppose a policy is regularized toward a coherent reference policy using matrix relative entropy. The optimum then has coherences that no diagonal reference policy produces, and its action probabilities can depend on the reference policy's coherences. This is relevant to fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs) with a Kullback--Leibler penalty. Second, suppose the agent chooses a unit-vector action and the reward is a quadratic function of that vector. This could arise when an LLM judge scores a weighted consolidation of reasoning paths, or when coupled robotic sensors each respond to a mix of actions. Then some coherent policies earn strictly more expected reward than every classical policy with the same action probabilities, and we give the margin in closed form. In a two-action example, both policies assign probability $0.5$ to each action, yet the classical one earns expected reward $0$ while the coherent one earns $1$, the maximum. Outside these two settings, DMRL matches or transfers the classical results. This is a theory paper. All results are proved, and we report no empirical evaluation.

Machine Learning.title: Soft MPCritic: Value-Based Reinforcement Learning for Non-Differentiable Predictive Control
Machine Learning.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) and model predictive control (MPC) offer complementary strengths, yet existing MPC-RL frameworks commonly rely on gradient-based optimization and therefore cannot handle the non-differentiable dynamics and objectives common in RL. We propose Soft MPCritic, an MPC-RL framework that learns a soft value function and uses sampling-based planning both for online control and for generating value targets. Specifically, Soft MPCritic instantiates MPC with model predictive path integral control (MPPI) and learns a terminal Q-function through fitted value iteration. Because the value targets are computed by the same planner used for control, the learned value function is aligned with the planner and implicitly extends its effective horizon. To keep target generation tractable, we introduce an amortized warm-start strategy that reuses the open-loop action sequences planned during online control to initialize batched MPPI computations of value targets, reducing computational cost without sacrificing solution quality. For robustness to model error, Soft MPCritic plans over scenarios drawn from an ensemble of dynamics models trained for next-step prediction. On both classical and constrained control tasks, Soft MPCritic learns effective policies with non-differentiable objectives, particularly where finite-horizon MPPI alone falls short. Soft MPCritic thus offers a practical blueprint for synthesizing MPC policies directly from black-box objectives, without differentiable surrogates.

Machine Learning.title: Online LLM Personalization from Pairwise Preferences Across Users
Machine Learning.summary: Large language models can answer the same question in different styles, but users' preferred styles are hidden and vary across users and questions. We study inference-time personalization through online selection from a fixed set of prompts, each representing a persona. Users arrive sequentially, each asks a short sequence of questions, and the system displays two responses per question and observes one pairwise choice. We formulate this interaction as a variant of the contextual dueling bandit problem in which the learner starts without preference data, adapts within each session, and exploits information shared across users. The objective is to minimize cumulative strong regret, summing the utility gaps of both displayed responses relative to the user's best response among the available options. We make two contributions. First, we introduce the problem and release a reproducible preference benchmark and dataset built around a tutoring case study, containing educational questions, LLM-generated answers in six teaching styles, and pairwise judgments from LLM-simulated students with hidden preference profiles. We fit Bradley-Terry models to these judgments to obtain reference utilities for regret evaluation. Second, we propose a baseline that learns a mixture prior over users from completed sessions and adapts to each new user within the session. On students and topics never used in development, it removes 44-48% of random pairs' excess regret and achieves over half the performance of a per-user linear oracle fitted in hindsight. We release code, prompts, and the benchmark.
Machine Learning.comment: 45 pages, 5 figures. Website: https://rogy-labs.github.io/tutorduel/ Code: https://github.com/RoGy-Labs/tutorduel-code Data: https://huggingface.co/datasets/romainpuech/tutorduel

Machine Learning.title: MLAfication: Efficiently Enabling High-Fidelity MLA for Modern LLMs
Machine Learning.summary: Multi-Head Latent Attention (MLA) compresses the KV cache into a latent representation, reducing inference memory and bandwidth. Existing MHA2MLA/TransMLA methods do not support QKNorm and require costly recovery on modern LLMs, especially MoE. We present MLAfication, a QKNorm-compatible, parameter-efficient extension of MHA2MLA. It combines calibrated KNorm, parameter-efficient distillation, contribution-aware Partial-RoPE, and activation-aware joint KV initialization. Across MHA and GQA models, including QKNorm- and MoE-equipped variants, MLAfication preserves performance under substantial KV-cache compression, surpasses the current SOTA on commonsense and long-context benchmarks, and extends MLA conversion to modern architectures. On Qwen3-30B-A3B, MLAfication delivers up to $5.35\times$ the serving throughput of BF16 GQA and, combined with 4-bit KV quantization, reduces the KV-cache footprint by $94.73\%$. Our code is available at https://github.com/JT-Ushio/MLAfication.

Machine Learning.title: FreeSolo: Linear-time Sparse Attention with Zero-Shot Length Extrapolation
Machine Learning.summary: Linear-time sequence models typically store long-context information in a recurrent state. A fixed-size state limits how much information can be stored, while hybrid architectures that add full attention for better recall incur quadratic sequence cost. Alternatively, sparse attention with continued pretraining (CPT) can extend the effective context length. Generalization beyond the trained length remains challenging, however, and CPT can be costly. We introduce FreeSolo, a native sparse attention mechanism with a short-range sliding window branch and a long-range branch that selects keypoint cells for direct token attention. Its linear-time variant, FS-L, learns to prune the prefix before query-dependent selection through short CPT. FS-B searches balanced trees with $O(N\log^2 N)$ algorithmic cost including radix-sort construction. FreeSolo demonstrates better zero-shot length extrapolation than the baselines without long-context fine-tuning.

Machine Learning.title: CartoVec: General-Purpose Location Embeddings from Open Map Data
Machine Learning.summary: Geographic coordinates are common inputs in applied machine learning, but latitude and longitude describe position rather than the surrounding environment. Image-grounded location encoders learn this context from satellite or ground-level imagery; structured open map data offers another source of supervision whose utility for continuous coordinate encoders remains less explored. We introduce CartoVec, a coordinate encoder trained to predict Overture-derived land cover, land use, transportation, place and connectivity targets at multiple spatial scales, without image inputs or downstream-task labels. We evaluate frozen embeddings on Census outcomes, Airbnb prices and Philadelphia crime in the US Northeast using spatial block cross-validation. CartoVec has the highest mean performance on most Census outcomes and the highest average across the full suite, with several comparisons close across folds. The findings support open map data as a practical source of reusable location representations with a coordinate-to-vector interface that requires no map lookup at inference. The open-weight model is available at https://huggingface.co/gursoyfurkan/CartoVec.

Machine Learning.title: Soft Teacher Forcing
Machine Learning.summary: Soft tokens have so far been used to replace discrete chain-of-thought in latent reasoning methods. These approaches typically require multi-stage training and, in some cases, auxiliary modules, yet they still underperform supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on <input, chain-of-thought, output> triples. In this paper, we ask whether soft tokens can be used to improve SFT itself, instead of as an avenue for latent reasoning. We introduce Soft Teacher Forcing (Soft-TF), a simple training algorithm that combines teacher-forced embeddings with soft tokens through random convex combinations. The soft tokens are computed in a single parallel forward pass over the ground-truth sequence. Soft-TF adds no parameters, no external model and no curriculum, and leaves inference unchanged. Experiments show that Soft-TF improves over SFT on GSM8K, MATH, MathQA and AQuA, by +2.1 to +4.1 points on GSM8K across seven Gemma, Llama and Mistral models.

Machine Learning.title: Convergence of Sharpness-Aware Minimization Algorithms using Increasing Batch Size and Decaying Learning Rate
Machine Learning.summary: The sharpness-aware minimization (SAM) algorithm and its variants, including gap guided SAM (GSAM), have been successful at improving the generalization capability of deep neural network models by finding flat local minima of the empirical loss in training. Meanwhile, it has been shown theoretically and practically that increasing the batch size or decaying the learning rate avoids sharp local minima of the empirical loss. In this paper, we consider the GSAM algorithm with increasing batch sizes or decaying learning rates, such as cosine annealing or linear learning rate, and theoretically show its convergence. Moreover, we numerically compare SAM (GSAM) with and without an increasing batch size and conclude that using an increasing batch size { achieves a lower worst-case $\ell_\infty$ adaptive sharpness} than compared with using a constant batch size and learning rate.

Machine Learning.title: ModRes: A modification of the ResPlan dataset ready for floor plan analysis and graph machine learning
Machine Learning.summary: Floor plan datasets underpin computational analysis of building layouts, spatial connectivity and graph machine learning. However, publicly available datasets often require substantial preprocessing before they can be used reliably. We present ModRes, a cleaned and enriched version of the ResPlan dataset, containing 8,431 valid and unique residential floor plans. Invalid and duplicate floor plans are removed through a dedicated cleaning workflow, producing a ready-to-use dataset. For each floor plan, ModRes provides two-dimensional geometry, images, three-dimensional building representations and three complementary dual graphs in CSV and JSON formats with graph-, node- and edge-level features. Continuous and categorical graph attributes support machine learning workflows. We characterise the dataset using graph-based statistics and demonstrate its utility through a range of case studies. ModRes provides structured geometric, topological and semantic representations needed to automate spatial analysis and support machine learning-based workflows for building design and performance evaluation.

Machine Learning.title: FunDM: Cheap & Label-Free Decision Models from Frozen Language Models
Machine Learning.summary: Decision models such as Jev score candidate answers or actions. A small decision head trained label-free can recover about 99% of a frozen language model's multiple-choice accuracy while using only two-thirds of its transformer layers. It learns the full model's answer probabilities with KL divergence, without correct-answer labels for training. One backbone pass reads the question and all options together; the head returns probabilities for every option. We call this model FunDM (Fun Decision Model). Using 24 of Qwen3-8B's 36 layers and skipping the LM head, its +1T variant reaches 75.0% mean accuracy over eight benchmarks, versus 75.7% for the full model. On MMLU-Pro, both heads achieve 1.56 to 1.57 times batched vLLM throughput with about one-third lower peak GPU allocator memory. Both heads score higher than released Contrastive Language Models (CLM), fine-tuned CLM, and CLM-shaped heads trained from scratch on the eight multiple-choice benchmarks and coding-agent selection. Separately trained agent heads learn judge probabilities without pass/fail labels and select passing runs for 74.4 to 74.6 of 100 held-out tasks on average, versus 74 for the full-model judge and 52.0 for a CLM-shaped action-trained head. Code is available at: https://github.com/Ujjawal-K-Panchal/FunDM

Machine Learning.title: Generative Flow on Symbolic Abstractions for Embodiment Capability Discovery
Machine Learning.summary: Achieving complex, long-horizon robot behavior remains challenging because successful execution depends on skills grounded in a robot's physical affordances. Existing training-task distributions are often handcrafted or sampled from large language models (LLMs), relying on semantic plausibility rather than embodiment-specific feasibility. This mismatch can produce curricula that are too difficult, redundant, or blind to non-obvious but learnable behaviors. We propose Generative Flow on Symbolic Abstractions (FOSA), a framework for discovering embodiment-specific capabilities by learning a grounded task generator. FOSA parameterizes an abstract policy as a Generative Flow Network that constructs symbolic task skeletons. Each skeleton is compiled into a simulation environment, where low-level policy-learning performance provides the reward signal for the abstract policy. Across heterogeneous robot platforms, FOSA discovers diverse and executable tasks near the robot's empirical capability frontier. After distilling the discovered task policies into a single language-conditioned policy, FOSA improves performance on unseen complex and long-horizon tasks. The code and demonstration videos are available at https://www.youwei-yu.com/fosa.
Machine Learning.comment: The code and demonstration videos are available at https://www.youwei-yu.com/fosa

Machine Learning.title: The Optimization Landscape of Carathéodory Decomposition of Toeplitz Covariances
Machine Learning.summary: Toeplitz covariance estimation is a classical signal processing problem, yet the geometry of the Gaussian maximum-likelihood objective remains only partially understood. Recent Newton-type, majorization-minimization, and gradient-based methods often solve the nonconvex problem globally with enough samples, but also reveal a difficult computational landscape. We study this phenomenon through an overparameterized Carathéodory representation, which parameterizes the covariance by the frequencies and amplitudes of steering vectors. A simple example shows that, for any uniform frequency grid, optimizing only the amplitudes can leave a positive error even in the population setting, which motivates optimizing the frequencies as well. Our main result proves that this nonlinear parameterization adds no stationary points: for any sample covariance, every stationary point with a positive definite covariance gives a stationary point of the Toeplitz maximum-likelihood problem. In the population setting, every such point therefore recovers the true covariance. We also prove that gradient descent converges to the true covariance in the population setting, and to the unique maximum likelihood estimate when the sample covariance is close enough to the true covariance. These results do not require overparameterization. Numerically, overparameterization speeds up gradient descent and gives a more accurate estimate for a fixed number of iterations.

Machine Learning.title: Detecting Multi-Agent Collusion Through Multi-Agent Interpretability
Machine Learning.summary: As LLM agents are increasingly deployed in multi-agent systems, they introduce risks of covert coordination that may evade standard forms of human oversight. While linear probes on model activations have shown promise for detecting deception in single-agent settings, collusion is inherently a multi-agent phenomenon, and the use of internal representations for detecting collusion between agents remains unexplored. We introduce NARCBench, a benchmark for evaluating collusion detection under environment distribution shift, and propose five probing techniques that aggregate per-agent deception scores to classify scenarios at the group level, evaluated across four open-weight models (Qwen3-32B, Llama-3.1-70B, DeepSeek-R1 32B, GPT-OSS-20B) and six probe architectures. We frame this as a distributed anomaly detection problem, identifying three collusion signatures that map onto distinct anomaly types and detection paradigms. Every model reaches 1.00 AUROC in-distribution; on our strongest model (Llama-3.1-70B), our five probing techniques achieve 0.73 to 0.93 AUROC when transferred zero-shot to structurally different multi-agent scenarios and 0.99 to 1.00 on a steganographic blackjack card-counting task, with detection performance scaling with model capability. We find that no single probing technique dominates across all collusion types, consistent with the framework's prediction that different anomaly types require different detection paradigms. This work takes a step toward multi-agent interpretability: extending white-box inspection from single models to multi-agent contexts, where detection requires aggregating signals across agents. These results suggest that model internals provide a complementary signal to text-level monitoring for detecting multi-agent collusion. Code and data available at https://github.com/aaronrose227/narcbench.

Machine Learning.title: Comprehensive Workflow for Uncertainty-Aware Ionic Liquid Solvent Discovery
Machine Learning.summary: Designing synthesizable materials with targeted properties remains one of the central objectives in materials sciences. Ionic liquids (ILs) are well suited to this goal due to their "tunability", where physical and chemical properties can be precisely customized by modifying their molecular structure, specifically by varying the combination of cations and anions. At the same time, current data-driven property models for ionic liquids often degrade in scarce, noisy, and uneven data regimes, where measurements cover only a small fraction of chemical space and a limited range of thermodynamic conditions. This makes out-of-distribution screening brittle: even when point predictions look plausible, it is difficult to compare candidates consistently, quantify downstream implications, or trust rankings enough to guide molecular discovery. We present a property-prediction and optimal candidate selection workflow that treats data processing, deep learning modeling, and physics-based calculations as a coupled system, linking property prediction with uncertainty estimation and physics-based filtering. By tightening the link between predicted properties and the criteria used for down-selection, the workflow supports reliable out-of-distribution ranking and enables prioritization of previously untested ionic liquid candidates with favorable predicted trade-offs. We demonstrate the application of our workflow by designing novel ionic liquids for CO2 capture from flue gas, predicting their properties and selecting Pareto-optimal candidates based on CO2 solubility, IL viscosity and working capacity.

Machine Learning.title: A Generalized McDiarmid Inequality: Sample Reuse and Non-Uniform Unbounded Differences
Machine Learning.summary: We develop a novel generalization of McDiarmid's concentration inequality and use it to obtain a uniform law of large numbers result and error bounds on stochastic optimization problems which simultaneously incorporate two key features: 1) They capture the benefit of training sample reuse in algorithms that also employ easily-sampled auxiliary random variables. 2) They allow for one-component mean-difference bounding functions which are both unbounded in the component of interest and have non-uniform dependence on another component. We demonstrate the utility of our method by deriving concentration inequalities for score-based generative modeling. This application naturally leverages both key features of our new tools: 1) It utilizes auxiliary Gaussian random variables in conjunction with the training samples; accounting for training sample reuse results in tighter error bounds by effectively integrating out the dependence on the auxiliary random variables. 2) The ability to handle non-uniform mean-difference bounding functions allows us to treat unbounded score models and data distributions with unbounded support.

Machine Learning.title: Neuromorphic Decoding and Dynamical Image Reconstruction from Populations of Spiking Retinal Ganglion Cells
Machine Learning.summary: Decoding visual stimuli from the spiking activity of retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) informs both our understanding of the retinal code and the design of visual prostheses. Natural vision is dynamic, yet state-of-the-art decoders mostly reconstruct single frames with artificial neural networks that process dense, continuous-valued signals rather than the retina's sparse, asynchronous spikes. We asked whether dynamic scenes can be reconstructed and tracked entirely within the spike domain, and at what computational cost. We built an end-to-end spiking neural network (SNN) whose neurons integrate the recorded RGC spikes over time. Populations of up to 1836 RGCs were recorded ex vivo from mouse retina on high-density microelectrode arrays while flashed images, moving bars, drifting gratings and randomly moving handwritten digits were presented. For moving digits, one shared spiking encoder fed two readouts, one reconstructing the image and one decoding the digit's position. Compute energy was estimated from counted synaptic operations. The SNN decoded what and where at once. It reconstructed the stimuli with a structural similarity (SSIM) of up to 0.93, refining the reconstruction as spikes accumulated, and tracked a randomly moving target with a mean error of 1.33 pixels on a $32\times32$ grid. Its fidelity nearly matched that of the best of 17 larger spiking and artificial decoders (5.9 million to 1.7 billion parameters, versus 5.4 million), and at a mean firing rate of 14.2% it needed an estimated $\sim$70-fold less compute energy than a dense artificial network of the same architecture. Dynamic visual scenes can thus be decoded from retinal population activity in the spike domain, with a compact network and at a compute cost compatible with implantable and wearable neural interfaces, supporting spike-native decoders for visual prostheses.

Machine Learning.title: Implicit and explicit reparameterizations of the Folded Normal and Rice distributions
Machine Learning.summary: Variational inference is a flexible tool for modeling experimental data and has proven useful in crystallography. Pathwise gradient estimators provide low-variance gradients for reparameterized variational inference, but are not readily available for some distributions central to crystallography. This work derives and implements implicit and explicit reparameterized gradient estimators for the folded Normal and Rice distributions in \prog{PyTorch}, and compares their variance analytically and empirically. In each case the implicit estimator achieves lower variance for the location derivative, particularly at small location-to-scale ratios, while the scale-derivative variances are nearly equal. For both distributions, implicit estimator is proved to be the conditional expectation of the explicit estimator given the sampled magnitude, so its variance is never larger. As a practical application, French-Wilson scaling is formulated as a variational inference problem, using the folded Normal and Rice distributions as variational families for centric and acentric reflections, respectively. Both estimators recover the exact posterior to better than $1\%$ on the amplitude, and converge at the same rate. The implementations are available in the open-source package \prog{rs-distributions}.
Machine Learning.comment: 45 pages, 14 figures, 3 tables. Includes supporting information (pages 29-45)

Machine Learning.title: SCOPE Before You Sample: Conformal Scores Guide Posterior Exploration for Fast and Calibrated Bayesian Predictive Inference
Machine Learning.summary: Bayesian predictive regions account for parameter uncertainty but can be poorly calibrated under model misspecification, even with expensive full MCMC. Cheaper approximations such as variational inference reduce the cost but often yield less accurate predictive distributions. We propose SCOPE (Score-guided Conformal Posterior Exploration), which retains the predictive quality of full MCMC while achieving calibrated coverage at a fraction of its cost. The key observation is that a prediction region can depend on the posterior mainly through a few parameter directions that move the region's boundary, and these are generally not the directions of largest posterior variance. SCOPE gives nonconformity scores a new role in guiding posterior computation: score gradients on a held-out guide set, weighted toward the target boundary, identify the relevant directions. MCMC explores this subspace, while an inexpensive projected variational approximation carries the remaining uncertainty. The same guide set calibrates the region's final density level. We establish asymptotic coverage for SCOPE and provide a split variant with finite-sample validity. Controlled simulations show that score-guided exploration yields more accurate calibrated regions than non-targeted direction choices at low active rank. Across simulated and real benchmarks, SCOPE has a median test-NLL gap of only 0.002 nats relative to full Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC), and on the real benchmarks it runs 12-15 times faster.

Machine Learning.title: OpenDGO: Benchmarking Multi-Agent Organizations Across Diverse Application Domains
Machine Learning.summary: Large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems are increasingly applied across diverse domains, yet different applications require different forms of agent organization. Existing studies typically adopt predefined organizations, such as Star, Chain, and Tree, or learn communication graphs to improve performance on specific tasks. However, these methods are largely designed and evaluated within a limited set of application domains, providing little understanding of whether an organization effective in one domain remains suitable for others with different collaboration requirements. We present \textbf{OpenDGO}, a controlled benchmark and analysis framework covering six real-world domains and three collaboration settings: Sequential Dependency, Parallel Decomposition, and Information Integration. Under matched tasks, agents, tools, and resource limits, OpenDGO compares fixed and learned organizations while separately examining communication graphs, role assignments, input assignments, resource budgets, and component failures. Our results show that there is no ``one-organization-for-all'' solution: preferred organizations vary across applications, and even the same communication graph can yield different outcomes under different role and input assignments. These findings highlight the need for application-dependent organization design, aiming to understand \emph{which organization is suitable for a given application, under what conditions, and why}.

Machine Learning.title: Masked Attention Pooling Is Invariant to Padding and Permutation: A Formal Proof in Lean
Machine Learning.summary: Attention-based multiple instance learning (MIL) pools a variable-size bag of instance embeddings into one vector. In batched training, bags are padded to a common length, and the pooled output is expected not to depend on how much padding was added or on the order in which instances are stored. This expectation holds only if padded rows are removed from both the numerator and the softmax normalizer. Common implementation idioms meet it only under side conditions. Zeroing padded features alone does not work. Masking logits with $-\infty$ fails on empty bags and on nonfinite padding. Masking with a large negative constant is exact only after floating-point underflow. We define masked attention pooling with a guarded normalizer and prove in Lean 4 with mathlib that it is invariant under any bijective reindexing of rows and under appending any finite number of masked rows with arbitrary real features and logits. We also prove that values at masked positions are irrelevant and that an all-masked bag maps to zero. The theorems hold for arbitrary finite index types and feature dimensions. Using the jax-lean certificate pipeline, we connect these theorems to the Jaxpr traced from the JAX kernel itself. Lean checks translation certificates for two concrete shapes, identifies the generated functions with the generic specification, and transfers both invariances to the imported Jaxpr's real-arithmetic semantics. All audited theorems depend only on Lean's three standard axioms. The results concern ideal real arithmetic. Floating-point execution, XLA, and the JAX tracer and importer remain outside the proof.

Machine Learning.title: Toward Agents That Reason About Their Computation
Machine Learning.summary: While reinforcement learning agents can achieve superhuman performance in many complex tasks, they typically do not become more computationally efficient as they improve. In contrast, humans gradually require less cognitive effort as they become more proficient at a task. If agents could reason about their compute as they learn, could they similarly reduce their computation footprint? If they could, we could have more energy efficient agents or free up compute cycles for other processes like planning. In this paper, we experiment with showing agents the cost of their computation and giving them the ability to control when they use compute. We conduct our experiments on the Arcade Learning Environment, and our results demonstrate that with the same training compute budget, agents that reason about their compute perform better on 75% of games. Furthermore, these agents use three times less compute on average. We analyze individual games and show where agents gain these efficiencies.
Machine Learning.comment: Accepted at the Reinforcement Learning Conference (RLC) 2026. Interactive version: https://adrianorenstein.com/paper/toward-compute

Machine Learning.title: Frequency-Aware Model Parameter Explorer: A new attribution method for improving explainability
Machine Learning.summary: State-of-the-art attribution methods such as AttEXplore rely on adversarial sample generation that applies an all-pass filter across the frequency spectrum: they perturb all frequencies of the input image alike, from the low frequencies that carry coarse shape to the high frequencies that carry edges and textures. However, models rely on low and high frequencies to different degrees, and such an all-pass perturbation cannot adapt to the model being explained, which limits the faithfulness of the resulting attribution maps. We propose FAMPE (Frequency-Aware Model Parameter Explorer), an attribution method that overcomes this limitation by perturbing the low- and high-frequency bands of the input independently, so that the perturbation can be shifted toward the band that matters for the model. The boundary between the two bands is set for each image automatically from its spectral energy. On ImageNet with five convolutional neural network and Vision Transformer architectures, FAMPE significantly improves the Insertion Score over the strongest baseline, AttEXplore, on four of them, by up to 15.4%, at essentially the same computational cost. How the perturbed frequency bands are weighted matters: the best and the worst balance between them differ by 19-36% in Insertion Score, and the best balance depends on the architecture. Choosing the balance for each image with a probe that needs no ground truth raises the Insertion Score significantly further on all five architectures, reaching up to 24.4% above AttEXplore. Controlling which frequency band is perturbed is therefore a simple, low-cost way to improve attribution faithfulness.

Machine Learning.title: Can Rényi Accountants Beat Lossless Accountants for DP-SGD?
Machine Learning.summary: Recent frameworks in differential privacy (DP), such as privacy loss distributions and $f$-DP, provide lossless representations of the privacy leakage of mechanisms. These approaches are often considered to yield tighter $(\varepsilon, δ)$-DP guarantees than those obtained from relaxed notions such as Rényi DP. But is that always the case? We study this question for differentially private stochastic gradient descent (DP-SGD) with fixed-size batches under replace adjacency. Our key observation is that in this setting, privacy accounting based on Rényi DP can use a pair of worst-case distributions (i.e., a dominating pair) that differs from the one used in the lossless frameworks. In particular, we characterize the worst-case distributions as two-dimensional Gaussian mixtures and derive an improved Rényi DP bound for DP-SGD. Numerical and asymptotic comparisons show that across various hyperparameter settings, a Rényi DP accountant based on the new bound can yield better privacy guarantees than those obtained from the lossless frameworks.

Machine Learning.title: When LLM Agents See a Conflict but Still Proceed: Cross-Domain Dependencies in Network Slicing
Machine Learning.summary: Future AI-native networks are being designed to apply autonomous agents built on large language models (LLMs) in network management through intents. When intents from different domains meet on the same resource, an agent must recognize the cross-domain dependency before taking an irreversible action. We investigate this problem through a smart-grid use case, in which a power utility holds an active intent on a backup slice for protection traffic. This slice appears idle by design, which is precisely the profile targeted by a cost-reduction intent. We built a tool-based environment in which the dependency must be either queried by the agent or read from an inventory annotation, together with a negative control, and evaluated ten models from four different providers in 600 runs. Most models acted against the dependency they had observed: seven of the ten models removed the protection slice at least once after receiving the cross-domain dependency, and in the high-harm tier the slice was removed in 76% of the exposed runs, while four models practically never did. Only one of ten models never removed the slice. We identify two failure modes, not querying the dependency and querying it but proceeding anyway, and show that agents often reported no conflict after observing it. These results indicate that, in AI-native networks, visibility of cross-domain dependencies is not a sufficient safeguard, and that dependency verification should be enforced by the management architecture before irreversible actions rather than delegated to the LLM's judgment.
Machine Learning.comment: Submitted to 11th Workshop on Communication Networks and Power Systems (WCNPS 2026)

Machine Learning.title: Gluing Local Contexts into Global Meaning: A Sheaf-Theoretic Decomposition of Transformer Representations
Machine Learning.summary: Existing interpretability tools do not test whether a representation keeps the same content when only the phrasing changes. We treat each paraphrase pair as a local witness that two activations should agree and build a cellular sheaf over the paraphrase graph; its Laplacian $L_\mathcal{F}$ answers the question on a frozen model with no training. The kernel $H^0$ is a content subspace: at 20 dimensions it beats the preserved subspace of the concept eraser LEACE on held-out CounterFact fact retrieval across eight architectures by a mean $+17.1$\,pp, and constraining all paraphrases of a fact jointly adds a further $+6.5$\,pp. The spectral complement concentrates causal influence: ablating the most paraphrase-variable coordinates, a coordinate-wise proxy for it, changes model outputs $5.6$ to $26.5\times$ more than ablating coordinates of matched per-coordinate variability, across nine models from 124M to 13B parameters. Stacking layers into a grid creates $b_1 = N(L-1)$ algebraic 1-cycles, and the resulting model-derived harmonic mass varies by nearly three orders of magnitude across six architectures and ranks them as their steering fragility does (Spearman $ρ= 0.90$, exact one-sided permutation $p = 0.014$). The same paraphrase graph yields the content subspace, the influence directions, and the fragility measure. Project page: https://cwru-aism.github.io/gluing-lc-page/
Machine Learning.comment: NeurIPS 2026 Poster, ICLR Unifying Concept Representation Learning

Machine Learning.title: Masked Diffusion for Travel Diaries Synthesis
Machine Learning.summary: Because household travel surveys combine household characteristics, variable-length person rosters, vehicle rosters, and trip chains, existing synthesis pipelines split them across separate models or flatten them into cropped fixed-length vectors. Representation, rather than modeling, becomes the bottleneck: splitting severs cross-segment dependence, and cropping truncates the household-structure distribution. We instead tokenize the diary and keep the object whole: each household-day becomes one token sequence with count tokens for vehicles, persons, and trips, and distinct symbols for padded, hidden, unobserved, and inapplicable positions. We introduce DiaryBridge, a masked diffusion model that bridges the fully hidden sequence to the distribution of complete diaries by unmasking positions in any order. One trained model, conditioned on any observed subset, performs synthesis and partial-diary completion alike. Experiments on real data extracted from the 2017/2018 Regional Travel Survey of the Baltimore region show that DiaryBridge generates travel reflecting vehicle availability and employment status, recovers shared trips using other household members' observed diaries, and better reproduces aggregate demand across modes, purposes, and departure periods than the learned baselines.

Machine Learning.title: LocalTrain: Integer-Only Local Learning for Energy-Efficient CNN Training on Edge FPGAs
Machine Learning.summary: Local learning reduces cross-layer training dependencies, but an efficient accelerator must still retain operands, accumulate gradients, and select quantization scales. We present an FPGA system that trains a CNN and its regional auxiliary classifiers using a shared integer matrix engine. Compact errors are expanded on chip, gradients are folded tile by tile, and historical scales permit direct output conversion. At 200 MHz, the KV260 prototype achieves 76.57% accuracy on CIFAR-10 and 91.85% on SVHN at approximately 4.20 W mean module power. Effective matrix throughput is 31.22 and 31.57 GMAC/s, respectively. Against the same integer method on Jetson Orin Nano, measured training energy is 40.4% and 42.1% lower, with $1.86\times$ and $1.82\times$ longer runtime; measurements use the respective platform power domains. Selected state checks and matching complete-run prediction counts support functional agreement with the software reference.

Machine Learning.title: Towards Universal Calibration for In-Context Classification
Machine Learning.summary: In-Context Learning (ICL) has received a lot of interest recently due to its ability to improve classification accuracy for new tasks without having to fine-tune the model over these tasks. However, the impact of ICL on calibration has been far less studied. Recent work has shown that ICL can have a negative impact on calibration due to biased selection of in-context examples. The existing methods for improving ICL calibration require additional task and model-specific training, detracting from the no-fine-tuning convenience of ICL. In this work, we introduce CALIBFORMER, a universal ICL calibrator for classification tasks, that generalizes to new models and tasks without further fine-tuning on these tasks. Specifically, we design a transformer-based calibrator which uses the model predictions on in-context examples to predict a confidence score for the test input. We show that the calibrator trained on three models and ten tasks, is able to generalize/calibrate ICL predictions on several new tasks and four LLMs unseen during training. Even for frontier models like Gemini, CALIBFORMER is able to obtain over 50% reduction in calibration error.
Machine Learning.comment: 30 pages, 11 figures, 19 tables, AACL-IJCNLP Findings accepted

Machine Learning.title: LoopQ: Quantization for Looped Language Models
Machine Learning.summary: Looped language models (LoopLMs) increase effective computational depth by repeatedly applying shared Transformer blocks without increasing the parameter count. However, this reuse makes them particularly sensitive to post-training quantization (PTQ). We systematically study PTQ in LoopLMs and identify three sources of degradation: distribution shift across roles, state reuse across loop transitions, and recursive error accumulation. We propose LoopQ, a loop-aware PTQ framework that preserves a shared quantized backbone while introducing lightweight adaptations. LoopQ combines loop-aware activation scaling and selective transformations to accommodate changing hidden-state distributions, cross-loop state alignment to stabilize transitions, and trajectory-aware calibration to limit accumulated error. Under W4A4 quantization, LoopQ achieves a 67.8% average relative improvement in five-task mean accuracy across four backbones and a conservative estimate of 75.2% for the average relative perplexity reduction across eight backbone-dataset pairs, compared with the strongest static PTQ baseline for each comparison.

Machine Learning.title: CMP: Robust Whole-Body Tracking for Loco-Manipulation via Competence Manifold Projection
Machine Learning.summary: While decoupled control schemes for legged mobile manipulators have shown robustness, learning holistic whole-body control policies for tracking global end-effector poses remains fragile against Out-of-Distribution (OOD) inputs induced by sensor noise or infeasible user commands. To improve robustness against these perturbations without sacrificing task performance and continuity, we propose Competence Manifold Projection (CMP). Specifically, we utilize a Frame-Wise Safety Scheme that transforms the infinite-horizon safety constraint into a computationally efficient single-step manifold inclusion. To instantiate this competence manifold, we employ a Lower-Bounded Safety Estimator that distinguishes unmastered intentions from the training distribution. We then introduce an Isomorphic Latent Space (ILS) that aligns manifold geometry with safety probability, enabling efficient O(1) seamless defense against arbitrary OOD intents. Experiments demonstrate that CMP achieves up to a 10-fold survival rate improvement in typical OOD scenarios where baselines suffer catastrophic failure, incurring under 10% tracking degradation. Notably, the system exhibits emergent "best-effort" generalization behaviors to progressively accomplish OOD goals by adhering to the competence boundaries. Project website: https://shepherd1226.github.io/CMP/
Machine Learning.comment: Accepted to CoRL 2026 (Spotlight). Project webpage: https://shepherd1226.github.io/CMP

Machine Learning.title: On the Upper Bounds for the Matrix Spectral Norm
Machine Learning.summary: We consider the problem of estimating the spectral norm of a matrix using only matrix-vector products. We propose a new Counterbalance estimator that provides upper bounds on the norm and derive probabilistic guarantees on its underestimation. Compared to standard approaches such as the power method, the proposed estimator produces significantly tighter upper bounds in both synthetic and real-world settings. Our method is especially effective for matrices with fast-decaying spectra, such as those arising in deep learning and inverse problems.

Machine Learning.title: Nearest Neighbor Functional Curve Completion for Intraday Probabilistic Revisions of Renewable Generation Forecasts
Machine Learning.summary: We propose a nonparametric approach that fuses deterministic initial forecasts and a partial realization into a probabilistic forecast using the framework of functional curve completion. Our motivation is to construct intra-day forecasts for renewable energy generation, which is a key operational task in modern power grids. The aim is to combine the day-ahead (DA) forecast and the morning realized generation profile to create trajectories for the rest of the day, quantifying operational uncertainty. Starting with a large database of complete forecast-actual pairs across many assets, we adopt a functional point of view and construct a weighted neighborhood based on similarity metrics for the observed partial curve, the DA forecast, the day, and the geographical location. The selected complete nearest-neighbor curves provide a full predictive distribution, including functional focal envelopes and predictive bands based on functional depth. The hyperparameters governing neighborhood size, distances, and fusion rates are tuned across forecast update times and directly target probabilistic calibration in terms of the predictive probability integral transform. Three case studies using synthetic wind and solar assets, as well as real-life regional wind generation, showcase that our algorithm is able to achieve excellent calibration.

Machine Learning.title: A Structural Theory of Position Bias in Transformers
Machine Learning.summary: Transformer models systematically favor certain token positions, yet the architectural origins of this position bias remain poorly understood. This bias is closely connected to the Lost-in-the-Middle phenomenon, where models underutilize information placed in the middle of the context. We show that causal Transformer architectures induce a systematic position-bias prior that can help explain the influence profiles associated with Lost-in-the-Middle. To characterize this prior, we develop a structural theory based on cumulative attention rollout with layerwise residual mixing. At finite depth, we isolate the competing positional drifts induced by causal masking, residual mixing, and positional encoding. Their interaction produces broad, often U-shaped profiles. At infinite depth, prior work predicts inevitable collapse under attention-only theory and identifies the discrepancy with observed Transformer behavior as an open problem. Under the stated boundedness assumptions, our residual-aware analysis replaces inevitable collapse with a dichotomy governed by cumulative attention mixing. Empirically, across 30 model-dataset settings, our adaptive residual-aware rollout closely matches measured input-token influence and reduces the average profile discrepancy by approximately 85% relative to both the attention-only and fixed-residual rollout baselines.
Machine Learning.comment: 32 pages, 6 figures, 9 tables. Revised and expanded version with improved presentation, residual-aware finite- and infinite-depth theory, RoPE experiments, broader model and dataset coverage, and additional validation and ablation studies

Machine Learning.title: The Value of Mechanistic Priors in Sequential Decision Making
Machine Learning.summary: Hybrid mechanistic models, physical priors with learned residuals, promise to reduce the data required for good decisions, but have no computable criterion to test this. We characterize the value of mechanistic priors in sequential decision-making within both asymptotic and burn-in regimes. To formalize this, we introduce the mechanistic information of a model: the mutual information between the model's recommended policy $\hatπ$ and the true optimal policy $π^*$, bounded via a centered, occupancy-weighted bias. In the asymptotic regime (large $N$), matched bounds reveal that Bayesian regret scales with the residual entropy $H_{\mathrm{mech}}$, delivering a theoretical sample complexity reduction of $H(μ)/H_{\mathrm{mech}}$ compared to an uninformed baseline. We further provide a computable pre-trial model certificate. Complementarily, in the clinically relevant burn-in regime (small $N$), we establish a lower bound on the penalty incurred by confidently wrong priors. We demonstrate both the asymptotic and burn-in bounds on an illustrative in-silico 5-fluorouracil (5-FU) chemotherapy plant whose structure follows published FOLFOX pharmacokinetics. The hybrid prior reduces cumulative regret by $1.79\times$ relative to standard body-surface-area dosing and $1.85\times$ relative to an uninformed learner, and remains below both under every calibration bias tested. Finally, we show that priors sensitive to distribution shift can lose half of their mechanistic information under a small distribution shift, motivating physically grounded priors for safety-critical applications.

Machine Learning.title: Novel Aspects of IEEE SA P3109 Arithmetic Formats for Machine Learning
Machine Learning.summary: The IEEE P3109 draft standard defines a parameterized family of binary floating-point formats and associated operations, with a focus on facilitating machine learning. These formats allow efficient and consistent representation of values in a small number of bits. The defined formats are parameterized over width and precision in bits, signedness, and the presence of infinities. Operations are defined by decoding floating-point values to the set of closed extended reals: the reals augmented with positive and negative infinity and NaN (Not a Number). Explicit treatment of NaN and infinite operands ensures that only real arithmetic is invoked in operation definitions. Extensive rounding and saturation modes are defined; stochastic rounding is included. Operations are exception-free, accelerating throughput, with exceptional situations communicated through return values, e.g., NaN. Operations on blocks of values sharing a common scale factor are defined in terms of the underlying operations in a uniform manner. System vendors may describe approximate implementations via a novel scale-invariant measure, akin to units in the last place. Standard function definitions and various other properties are mechanically verified and generated using formal specifications.

Machine Learning.title: Sampling from multimodal distributions with warm starts: Non-asymptotic bounds for the Reweighted Annealed Leap-Point Sampler
Machine Learning.summary: Sampling from multimodal distributions is a central challenge in Bayesian inference and machine learning. In light of hardness results for sampling -- classical MCMC methods, even with tempering, can suffer from exponential mixing times -- a natural question is how to leverage additional information, such as a warm start point for each mode, to enable faster mixing across modes. To address this, we introduce Reweighted ALPS (Re-ALPS), a modified version of the Annealed Leap-Point Sampler (ALPS) that dispenses with the Gaussian approximation assumption. We prove the first polynomial-time bound that works in a general setting, under a natural assumption that each component contains significant mass relative to the others when tilted towards the corresponding warm start point. Similarly to ALPS, we define distributions tilted towards a mixture centered at the warm start points, and at the coldest level, use teleportation between warm start points to enable efficient mixing across modes. In contrast to ALPS, our method does not require Hessian information at the modes, but instead estimates component partition functions via Monte Carlo. This additional estimation step is crucial in allowing the algorithm to handle target distributions with more complex geometries besides approximate Gaussian. For the proof, we show convergence results for Markov processes when only part of the stationary distribution is well-mixing and estimation for partition functions for individual components of a mixture.

Machine Learning.title: TILE: Bridging LLMs and Table Foundation Models for Tabular Learning with Strings
Machine Learning.summary: Real-world tables are often heterogeneous, combining numerical features with free-form string columns. Table foundation models (TFMs) excel on numerical tables but require strings to be encoded numerically, while large language models (LLMs) hold semantic knowledge but are not designed for tabular predictions. Most existing bridges use LLMs as plug-in encoders for cell strings, yet how to extract representations effectively for tabular learning remains underexplored. We show that the interface between LLMs and tables matter as much as the LLM itself. Applied cell-wise, larger LLMs do not give better features. With our interface, the same LLMs improve steadily with size. TILE (Table-Interfaced LLM Embeddings) combines four ingredients: row serialization to provide cross-column context, intermediate-layer extraction to avoid layers specialized for next-token prediction, columnar pooling to remove mean pooling's length bias, and by-pass features to route numbers and categories past the LLM. Paired with TFMs, TILE sets a new state of the art for tables with strings. Across 100 datasets, it beats the strongest baseline on 89% of splits, with gains across 7 LLMs and 10 tabular learners, and ranks first on the 108-dataset STRABLE benchmark.

Machine Learning.title: Gradient Routing Localizes and Removes Unintended Behaviors in RL
Machine Learning.summary: We propose a mitigation to reward hacking in reinforcement learning. Our setup involves a misspecified reward function that gives rise to unintended behavior, and a monitor used to detect unintended behavior. As with frontier AI systems, the monitor makes systematic errors. Consequently, using the monitor for data filtering or to apply a reward penalty fails to prevent the model from learning unintended behavior ("reward hacking"). To address this problem, we introduce GRAFT: Gradient Routing Adapter Fine Tuning. Rather than penalizing or filtering flagged samples during training, GRAFT constrains gradient updates on those samples to a sacrificial set of new parameters. This has two benefits: First, because the monitor is not part of the reward function, the model does not learn to hide misbehavior. Second, ablating the sacrificial parameters reduces or entirely stops the unintended behavior while maintaining improved performance on target tasks. We demonstrate these benefits in RL environments where reward penalties cause models to learn to reward hack in undetected ways, training models ranging from 135M to 8B parameters. Additionally, we show a similar effect at a larger scale by distilling frontier LLM trajectories containing reward hacking into Qwen3-32B, without teaching that model to reward hack. Overall, our work suggests GRAFT may be a promising approach for leveraging imperfect monitors during post-training in settings where true performance is difficult to evaluate.

Machine Learning.title: In-context classification: Calibration and noise in linear attention with softmax readout
Machine Learning.summary: We study in-context binary classification in a simple attention model trained to minimise a logistic loss. Each prompt has a latent logistic teacher, and the learner must infer its direction from Bernoulli-labeled context examples. We derive an asymptotic prediction for the test logit in a high-dimensional regime with context length proportional to token dimension, and total training prompts proportional to dimension squared. Our formula cleanly separates calibration, test-time context noise, and non-isotropic parameter-estimation noise as interpretable effects on in-context performance. Our analysis also identifies the ridgeless separability regime and addresses the effects of context length, pretraining-set size, regularisation, and sampling temperature on in-context classification performance. The theory's predictions closely agree with finite-dimensional simulations and fully trained linear-attention models, while experiments with standard softmax attention show qualitatively related behaviour beyond the regime assumed by our analysis.

Machine Learning.title: Measuring Variable Importance Using Proportional Inclusive Marginal Effects
Machine Learning.summary: Shapley-based measures are widely used for measuring variable importance in statistics and machine learning. However, these measures have a serious issue--a nonactive variable can get a positive importance measure when it is correlated with an active variable. Herin et al. recently proposed a measure called proportional marginal effects (PME) that mitigates this spurious effect. However, PME is developed for deterministic models and has high computational cost. In this article, we propose a new measure called proportional inclusive marginal effects (PRIME) that overcomes these two limitations of PME. The key idea in PRIME is to use a novel model-free variable selection technique to identify the active variables and include only them in the computation of the importance measure. Analysis of test functions and real datasets show that PRIME can accurately and reliably quantify variable importance from noisy input-output data.

Machine Learning.title: Is Complex Query Answering Really Complex?
Machine Learning.summary: Complex query answering (CQA) on knowledge graphs (KGs) is gaining momentum as a challenging reasoning task. In this paper, we show that the current benchmarks for CQA might not be as complex as we think, as the way they are built distorts our perception of progress in this field. For example, we find that in these benchmarks, most queries (up to 98% for some query types) can be reduced to simpler problems, e.g., link prediction, where only one link needs to be predicted. The performance of state-of-the-art CQA models decreases significantly when such models are evaluated on queries that cannot be reduced to easier types. Thus, we propose a set of more challenging benchmarks composed of queries that require models to reason over multiple hops and better reflect the construction of real-world KGs. In a systematic empirical investigation, the new benchmarks show that current methods leave much to be desired from current CQA methods.

Machine Learning.title: Energy per Successful Goal: Goal-Level Energy Accounting for Agentic AI Systems
Machine Learning.summary: Current AI energy benchmarks measure consumption per model invocation. For agentic systems, where a single user goal may trigger multistep orchestration, tool calls, retries, and failure recovery, the invocation count is an implementation artifact rather than a task property, and per inference normalization misrepresents the energy cost of completing a goal. We present A-LEMS (Agentic LLM Energy Measurement System), a cross layer framework that redefines the unit of AI energy accounting as Energy per Successful Goal (EpG): total workflow energy across all attempts, including failures and retries, divided by successfully completed goals. A-LEMS combines a temporal boundary model, a five layer attribution pipeline mapping hardware signals (RAPL on x86; SPBM and DCGM on ARM) to workflow energy, and a reproducibility protocol binding every measurement to hardware, environment, and runtime configuration. Building on EpG, we define the Orchestration Overhead Index (OOI), the ratio of agentic to linear EpG on matched goals under identical success criteria. Across nine task families on Intel x86 and NVIDIA Grace GB10 ARM, CPU only OOI ranges 0.35x to 11.07x. Including GPU dynamic energy, which accounts for 83.8% of agentic EpG in local inference, widens this to 0.4x to 26.48x, so CPU only measurement understates overhead about twofold for reasoning tasks. For remote inference, network wait energy shifts OOI from 2.5x to 2.35x. The overhead arises from orchestration structure (planning, retries, recovery) that induces additional inference calls, not from costlier individual calls. The metric is not biased upward: single tool calculator dispatch inverts to OOI = 0.61x (95% CI [0.35, 0.97]) on x86. Goal level accounting via EpG and OOI provides a measurement foundation for benchmarking agentic AI.
Machine Learning.comment: v2: 37 pages. Adds ARM platform (NVIDIA Grace GB10) with GPU (DCGM) and network wait energy, nine task families, bootstrap confidence intervals, stochastic retry model, and new coauthors

Machine Learning.title: Learning to Test: Latent Representation Learning for Dynamic Instability Detection
Machine Learning.summary: Stability assessment is central to safety-critical systems governed by differential-algebraic equations (DAEs), whose dynamics are constrained by physical laws and admissibility conditions. These systems operate under stochastically varying environmental inputs, so stability must be reassessed as the context distribution shifts, yet repeated large-scale DAE simulation is prohibitive in high-dimensional or real-time settings. We propose a test-oriented learning framework that tests a trajectory-level chance constraint from deployment contexts alone. Rather than re-estimating physical parameters or re-solving the DAE, we learn a latent representation from baseline context-trajectory data that retains stability-relevant information and is regularized toward a tractable reference distribution, and calibrate a latent discrepancy test over the composite safety null. We establish exact validity for oracle calibration and asymptotic validity for its empirical implementation under class-conditional latent invariance, and show that the guarantee degrades gracefully when this invariance holds only approximately. On simulated dynamical systems and a power-system real-world example, our approach strikes a balance between validity and power, whereas other baseline methods each fail in at least one regime. An ablation that injects controlled violations of the invariance assumption shows that decisions stay correct while the violation is below the safety margin, as the theory predicts.

Machine Learning.title: MENTOR: Procedural Shielding of Tool-Using LLM Agents
Machine Learning.summary: Tool-using LLM agents are increasingly used to automate workflows governed by procedural manuals, such as company rules for booking travel or procuring hardware. These manuals are written in natural language for humans and describe general requirements over such complex workflows. Ensuring compliance of LLM agents with these manuals is difficult, and state-of-the-art techniques use either LLM judges or manually written rules to forbid problematic tool-calls locally at runtime. This is insufficient because (i) only blocking tool calls keeps the agent clueless about how to make correct progress towards fulfilling its task, and (ii) can lead to overly conservative behavior of the agent, as tool calls might only be problematic in certain contexts. To overcome these challenges, we introduce MENTOR, which (i) additionally provides guidance for the agent to make procedural-compliant progress on the task, and (ii) ensures that this compliance is context-aware. We achieve these goals by building a novel history-dependent runtime shield that is obtained from the procedural manual via a multi-step autoformalization pipeline. At its core, MENTOR utilizes a game-based technique to ensure robustness against runtime uncertainty without over-resticting agents' behavior. This yields a formally assisted framework for procedural shielding of LLM agents that improves compliance well beyond existing methods. In particular, MENTOR lifts the compliance of shielded light-weight open-source LLMs above that of non-shielded proprietary models. Since a shield is synthesized once per manual and then serves every task, a MENTOR-shielded agent becomes a viable choice for repeatedly executed workflows, potentially reducing deployment costs when the offline construction cost is amortized over repeated tasks.

Machine Learning.title: Honeycomb Crystal in a Mass-Asymmetric Electron-Hole Bilayer
Machine Learning.summary: A two-dimensional electron gas in a uniform neutralizing background forms a triangular Wigner crystal at low density. In a strongly mass-asymmetric electron-hole bilayer, localized heavy holes instead provide a nonuniform positive background that supports an electron crystal at densities two orders of magnitude higher than for a homogeneous electron gas in the same material. Here we show that correlated mobile electrons can overturn the preference for triangular order, stabilizing a honeycomb electron-hole crystal. Using the powerful real-space neural-network variational Monte Carlo in the Born-Oppenheimer limit with fixed holes, we find that increasing the density drives a transition from a triangular electron-hole crystal to a honeycomb crystal, which eventually melts into itinerant electrons coexisting with the honeycomb or the triangular hole lattice at fixed interlayer separation. Relative to triangular order, honeycomb order emerges when gains in electronic kinetic energy and electron-hole attraction outweigh its higher intralayer Coulomb repulsion, a threshold never reached in the rigid point-dipole model. Moreover, the honeycomb hole lattice supports paramagnetic, antiferromagnetic, and stripe-ordered spin states. Complex polarization indicates a metal-insulator transition, while the states on the honeycomb hole lattice are consistent with a stripe-ordered Dirac semimetal and paramagnetic or antiferromagnetic Mott insulators via mapping to the half-filled Hubbard model. We further propose a BLG/hBN/WS$_2$-WSe$_2$ heterostructure as a platform for the predicted honeycomb crystal, at an experimentally feasible density $n\sim10^{11}~\text{cm}^{-2}$.

Machine Learning.title: SPLICE: Sparse Physics Library Identification and Compositional Expansion
Machine Learning.summary: Neural operator splitting composes a library of neural operators, one per physical mechanism, into zero-shot simulators of new equations. Existing approaches, however, require these mechanisms and their labels to be specified in advance. We ask whether a pretrained library can instead be adapted and grown from unlabeled trajectories in which multiple mechanisms act simultaneously. We introduce SPLICE, a framework that discovers operators without mechanism labels on mixture data. The contributions of the candidate operators to each trajectory are inferred by solving a convex optimization problem. A calibrated test then assigns each discovered operator the mechanism it implements. Failure cases are also detectable, when the library lacks the required physics or when mechanisms are insufficiently separable. Across one and two dimensional systems, the discovered operators recover mechanisms from unlabeled mixtures and compose into zero-shot simulators of unseen equations; a frozen library can also grow an operator for physics absent from pretraining, without labels and without forgetting. On Navier-Stokes, the discovered operators compose about as accurately as their supervised counterparts.

Machine Learning.title: Generative Conformal Prediction with Optimized Coverage Allocation
Machine Learning.summary: Conformal prediction provides model-agnostic uncertainty quantification with guaranteed coverage, but conventional methods often yield overly conservative uncertainty sets, particularly in multimodal or heterogeneous settings. This inefficiency arises from two sources: (i) limited expressiveness of the predictive model and (ii) simplistic nonconformity score design. Most existing approaches advance only one of these axes, leaving the other underexplored. We propose generative conformal prediction with Optimized Ranking and Coverage Allocation (ORCA), a three-stage framework that advances both aspects jointly. ORCA leverages generative models to capture the full conditional distribution and introduces a rank-dependent optimization procedure that adaptively allocates coverage for efficiency while maintaining validity. We cast this coverage allocation as an optimization problem, derive an exact mixed-integer linear programming formulation, and show that the solution converges asymptotically to the oracle density-level set. Across synthetic, semi-synthetic, and real datasets, ORCA produces substantially more efficient uncertainty sets than state-of-the-art baselines, demonstrating robust gains in scenarios where conventional conformal prediction methods fail.

Machine Learning.title: Less Noise, Same Certificate: Retain Sensitivity for Unlearning
Machine Learning.summary: Certified machine unlearning aims to provably remove the influence of a deletion set $U$ from a model trained on a dataset $S$, by producing an unlearned output that is statistically indistinguishable from retraining on the retain set $R := S\setminus U$. Many existing certified unlearning methods adapt techniques from Differential Privacy (DP) and add noise calibrated to global sensitivity, i.e., the worst-case output change over all adjacent datasets. We show that this DP-style calibration is often overly conservative: unlike DP, unlearning requires no indistinguishability across different retain sets, only between each deletion output and retraining on the same retain set $R$. Motivated by this distinction, we define retain sensitivity as the worst-case output change over deletions $U'$ from $R\cup U'$ while keeping $R$ fixed. While insufficient for DP, retain sensitivity is exactly sufficient for unlearning, allowing for the same certificates with less noise. We validate these reductions in noise theoretically and empirically across several problems, including the weight of minimum spanning trees, PCA, and ERM. Finally, we refine the analysis of two widely used certified unlearning algorithms through the lens of retain sensitivity, leveraging the regularity induced by $R$ to further reduce noise and improve utility.

Machine Learning.title: Understanding Personalization Gains in Whisper
Machine Learning.summary: Whisper-style ASR models provide strong zero-shot transcription, but their residual errors are not evenly distributed across datasets, recording conditions, and metadata-based groups. We study when lightweight low-rank adaptation (LoRA) improves Whisper and whether observed gains require group-specific adapters. Across Common Voice, LibriSpeech, and VoxPopuli, we compare zero-shot Whisper, pooled LoRA, and group-specific LoRA under matched within-group splits. We find that adaptation is not uniformly beneficial: gains are concentrated in difficult Common Voice groups, are consistent on VoxPopuli, and largely disappear on low-error LibriSpeech. Crucially, pooled LoRA often matches, and sometimes clearly outperforms, group-specific LoRA. Gains over zero-shot should therefore be tested against matched pooled adaptation before being interpreted as evidence of personalization.

Machine Learning.title: LLM Evaluation is a Forecasting Problem
Machine Learning.summary: Standard procedure in machine learning is to randomly split train and test data, emulating IID draws from one underlying data distribution. In practice, models are trained on past data and deployed in the future, which may come from distinct distributions. In this paper, we find that web text is indeed highly non-stationary, as text distributions shift over time. We further observe that model performance changes continuously over time across diverse benchmarks. Consequently, future model performance is better predicted by measurements made on recent evaluation data, and is best predicted by time series forecasters applied to historic performance rather than by historic performance itself. Choosing which model to deploy based on forecasted accuracy enables more reliable selection of performant models, thus improving downstream accuracy in the regime practitioners care about: deployment. Taken together, our experiments suggest that time should be treated as a fundamental variable in LLM evaluation. We release our code and data.

Machine Learning.title: ProbabilityBench: Model Evaluation and Calibration with Exact Ground-Truth Uncertainty
Machine Learning.summary: Evaluating model uncertainty on real-world data is challenging because each instance provides only a single observed label, leaving true conditional class probabilities unknown. To address this, we introduce ProbabilityBench, a benchmark that provides exact, instance-level class probabilities across three simulated text-based domains: peer review, covert information transfer, and credit risk. By explicitly defining the full data-generating process for each environment, we analytically compute both exact class probabilities and Bayes error. Furthermore, we provide a theoretical guarantee that rendering these cases into natural-language memos strictly preserves their underlying generative probabilities. This exactness enables direct measurement of reported probability quality via KL divergence. Across 16 evaluated models, most models on the observed cost-quality Pareto frontiers are decision models, including Jev and Perplexity Decider. Finally, ProbabilityBench serves as a meta-evaluation framework, leveraging known ground-truth values to benchmark the accuracy of standard calibration metrics and Bayes-error estimators themselves.

Machine Learning.title: MAGNET: Manifold-Aware Graph Diffusion Network for Connectome Generation
Machine Learning.summary: Functional brain connectome represents neural connectivity as a matrix of pairwise interactions between brain regions. Generation of functional connectomes is not only a question of validity; rather, having satisfied the constraints on the correlation matrix, the next step is to recover the class-conditional geometry buried under coarse labels. We propose MAGNET, a Manifold-Aware Graph Diffusion Network which uses a normalized-Cholesky representation of the manifold of correlation matrices that guarantees validity. MAGNET lifts noisy latent states into ROI-level region tokens and performs denoising with a relational inductive bias over brain atlas regions. To deal with structural problems induced by coarse labels, MAGNET employs class-anchored conditioning, amortized structural bridge, and relevance-preserving corruption. Across ABIDE, ADNI, and OASIS-3, MAGNET consistently achieves favorable results compared to previous manifold-aware approaches, demonstrating improvements of 7-21% in class-conditional fidelity ($α,β$-F1) across three cohorts and better sampling efficiency. Moreover, while training only with strict binary labels, MAGNET is capable of maintaining clinical heterogeneity through fine substructure of the connectomes in a zero-shot setting, improving subclass covariance alignment ($λ$-MSE) by over 30%. These results suggest that geometric validity is a necessary but insufficient condition for clinical utility in connectome synthesis. Moreover, efforts in making the diffusion denoising class-conditional manifold aware finds utility beyond the highly curved brain connectome generation as this is a critical problem in various general settings. The code repository can be found at https://github.com/protyayofficial/MAGNET.

Machine Learning.title: Targeted Active Learning for Preference-Based Treatment Effects on Multivariate Outcomes
Machine Learning.summary: Treatment efficacy is traditionally demonstrated on the basis of a single primary outcome. However, clinical decision-making usually requires consideration of multiple outcomes, balancing expected benefits against potential risks. The relative value assigned to these outcomes varies substantially from one patient to another. Given a preference rule over outcome profiles, treatment effects and optimal policies can be defined and estimated. Such a rule is rarely available in practice: it must itself be estimated from pairwise comparisons of outcome profiles, which are costly to collect from clinical experts. We propose an active learning framework that selects which comparisons to query. Standard criteria maximize the information gained on the preference rule itself. We instead target the quantities of interest, and select the query that most reduces uncertainty on the treatment effect and on the optimal policy induced by the learned rule. Under a Gaussian process model of the preference rule, we derive a closed-form approximation of this criterion. On semi-synthetic data built from a Parkinson's disease cohort with 13 clinical outcomes, our criterion achieves lower treatment effect estimation error and lower policy regret than existing criteria at equal query budget.

Machine Learning.title: Mixture of GFlowNets
Machine Learning.summary: Generative Flow Networks (GFlowNets) learn a policy that samples compositional objects in proportion to an unnormalized reward $R(x)$. This makes them useful wherever many diverse, high-reward candidates are needed and oracle queries are expensive. In practice, a single GFlowNet often fails to cover all modes of a complex distribution, and the obvious ways to scale compute saturate: larger batches and data-parallel gradient averaging draw every trajectory from one, possibly biased, policy, so extra rollouts rediscover known modes instead of finding new ones. We explore whether this mode-bias problem (mode collapse in the extreme) can be addressed with a population of asynchronously trained policies which divide the state space between them. Mixture of GFlowNets (MoG) replaces the single forward policy with a community of $K$ independent GFlowNets coupled through one jointly trained soft classifier, which assigns each member its own region of the state space through reward shaping. Mixing the members under their learned partition functions provably recovers the target $p(x)\propto R(x)$. MoG exchange (MoGX) also lets the classifier route sampled trajectories: a trajectory the classifier assigns to another member is sent to that member and trained on there, with no importance sampling. We evaluate both methods by keeping the environment-interaction budget fixed while scaling the community size, turning parallel compute into mode coverage without extra oracle calls. On HyperGrid, across six reward landscapes and communities of up to $K{=}64$, MoG and MoGX keep finding new modes as $K$ grows, while data-parallel training saturates.
