Each robot broadcasts the perceptual latent vector it already computes for its own use, the output of an encoder trained with a self-supervised joint-embedding predictive objective, frozen, and shared across the team. A teammate learns to act on it from task reward alone. Because the encoder already runs for perception, the message costs no additional computation and a single compact vector of bandwidth. Because the encoder is frozen before any policy is trained, the message means the same thing to every robot, and the receiving robot is never told what it means. We evaluate Latent Telepathy with a content-controlled protocol in which bandwidth, latency, topology and receiver are held fixed and only the message content varies. Broadcasting the latent lets a navigator avoid an occluded hazard in 99.7% of episodes, matching a noiseless hand-designed message. Position and trajectory messages remain at chance, and the raw camera image, 186 times wider, is less reliable than the compressed latent. The result holds from a discrete gridworld to rendered pixels under continuous velocity control, and the encoder decodes the hazard from a physical robot's camera in 102 of 102 live decisions. We also identify a requirement for porting MARL communication results to continuous control, that the decision a message informs must remain reachable by exploration, and show how to restore it.
Machine Learning.comment: 8 pages, 6 figures. Submitted to IEEE ICRA 2027

Machine Learning.title: Fast Quantized Johnson$-$Lindenstrauss Transforms
Machine Learning.summary:
Quantization has emerged as one of the primary techniques for reducing the memory footprint of large language models during inference. A prominent example is Quantized Johnson$-$Lindenstrauss (QJL), which compresses KV caches using 1-bit asymmetric quantization while approximately preserving the inner products required by the attention mechanism. Recent theoretical and practical work aims at replacing the dense Gaussian projections used by the aforementioned transforms with more structured embeddings $-$ such as compositions of randomized Hadamard transforms $-$ while retaining the same embedding dimension.
  In this paper, we introduce two constructions based on a composition of randomized Hadamard transforms, albeit with a Gaussian rather than Rademacher diagonal in the second stage. The first adds Gaussian dithering to smooth the quantizer, while the second inserts a random permutation to regularize the covariance structure of the resulting Gaussian measurements.
  We prove embedding-dimension and running-time guarantees analogous to those of Fast JL in the non-quantized setting. The first construction achieves $m=O(\varepsilon^{-2}\log^2(d/δ))$, while the second achieves $m=O(\varepsilon^{-2}\log(d/δ))$ under a restriction on $m$. Both constructions can be applied in $O(d\log d)$ time.

Machine Learning.title: Moment-Based Anomaly Detection in High-Dimensional Mixed Data
Machine Learning.summary: We propose an anomaly detection method for high-dimensional mixed-type data that maps heterogeneous features to a common scale via standardized moment-based transformations, yielding interpretable feature-level anomaly scores. These scores are combined through a dependence-aware aggregation step to construct the Mixed-data Influence (MDI) score, accounting for correlations across features and providing a unified measure of how strongly an observation departs from the reference data distribution. By incorporating higher-order moments, the MDI can detect anomalies that arise not only from location shifts, but also from changes in variability, skewness, and other distributional characteristics. The aggregation mechanism allows our method to capture both sparse anomalies concentrated in a small number of features and weak, coordinated deviations distributed across many features. We empirically investigate the distribution and thresholding behavior of the MDI score across different sample sizes, dimensions, dependence structures, and data types. Simulation experiments and two real-data applications, to multi-omics and ESG data, evaluate finite-sample calibration, detection performance, and feature-level interpretability.

Machine Learning.title: agent-risk: Risk Assessment for Changes to AI Agents
Machine Learning.summary: Before changing a deployed AI agent (a stricter safety gate, a new model), organizations must approve the change, starting from existing logs. Extending classical risk analysis to partial records and partial changes to running systems, agent-risk replays logged episodes, assuming nothing else changes and the agent does not anticipate the change. The log settles episodes acting as before, a declared stop value settles stopped ones, and the rest need logged support, a saved-state rerun, or a bound. We prove what logs must record for exact replay and which saved states serve a gate family. For independent episodes, we bound the reruns a decision needs and tolerable drift from live behavior. In a bash sandbox, a 7,200-episode log alone decided neither of two retry gates, which let the agent act after refusals the log never shows. Rerunning only each gate's blocked episodes from saved states reached both live decisions at half the agent calls of a live test sized post hoc for them, given the log. Without per-step harm, a stopping gate's certified harm ceiling rose up to 2.5-fold, since the log hides whether harm preceded the stop. Approval thus needs evidence designed in advance: log fields, saved states, targeted reruns.
Machine Learning.comment: 43 pages, 5 figures, 7 tables. Code, registrations, and logs: https://github.com/yzhao062/agent-risk

Machine Learning.title: A Survey of Flow Matching in Reinforcement Learning
Machine Learning.summary: Flow Matching (FM) has recently emerged as a principled and efficient generative modeling framework for reinforcement learning (RL), enabling expressive, multimodal policy parameterizations via deterministic probability transport. Compared to diffusion-based policies that rely on stochastic denoising chains, FM uses sampling based on ordinary differential equations (ODEs), with learned velocity fields, which can substantially reduce inference latency and simplify the incorporation of RL objectives. As research in flow-based RL rapidly accelerates across offline continuous control, online fine-tuning, and foundation model alignment, the literature has become highly fragmented. In this survey, we provide a comprehensive taxonomy of flow-matching approaches in reinforcement learning. We organize the literature along two axes: the target distribution being modeled (e.g., action policies, value critics, transition dynamics) and the mechanism of RL signal integration (e.g., energy-weighted regression, flow-based policy gradients, and group relative policy optimization). Furthermore, we survey emerging frontiers such as discrete and non-Euclidean action spaces, provide a systematic comparative analysis against Gaussian and diffusion baselines, and outline critical open problems. Ultimately, this survey serves as a foundational roadmap for the next generation of generative reinforcement learning and alignment.
Machine Learning.comment: 52 pages. Published in Transactions on Machine Learning Research (TMLR), 2026. Survey Certification. Reviewed on OpenReview: https://openreview.net/forum?id=P6e5IC4gPe

Machine Learning.title: On the Relaxation of Conditional Independence Assumption for Image Segmentation
Machine Learning.summary: In semantic segmentation, a recent line of RankSEG methods directly optimizes Dice/IoU scores at inference time, improving alignment with evaluation metrics without modifying model training. Despite its theoretical and empirical success, RankSEG relies on the restrictive Conditional Independence Assumption (CIA), which ignores crucial label correlations and therefore degrades performance in ambiguous or low-contrast scenarios. However, accounting for full label dependence is computationally prohibitive, requiring $\mathcal{O}(d^3)$ time. To address this, we replace the CIA with a Spatially Localized Dependence (SLD) structure that captures local label correlations while keeping the dependence model tractable. We further overcome the remaining computational bottleneck via a Reciprocal Moment Approximation coupled with a novel fixed-point optimization strategy that eliminates exhaustive search. The proposed algorithm achieves a highly practical $\mathcal{O}(d \log d)$ complexity and consistently outperforms conventional argmax and CIA-based RankSEG across diverse segmentation benchmarks. Improvements are significant in low-contrast or small-object scenarios, where label dependence offers valuable signals complementary to image information for accurate segmentation. The code of experiments is available at https://github.com/ZixunWang/RankSEG-DEP.

Machine Learning.title: Deep Speech Representations Track Word Timing along a Low-Dimensional Circular Trajectory
Machine Learning.summary: Speech timing is fundamental for speech models to recognize words accurately, but how word-timing information is represented in speech models remains underexplored. We study this question using the framework of representational geometry, which investigates whether and how concepts are represented in low-dimensional subspaces of the representation space. Prior work in cognitive neuroscience has shown that when HuBERT feature sequences are averaged across words of the same duration, they form near-circular trajectories from word onset to word offset in a two-dimensional "temporal subspace." Here we show that this circular structure of word timing is a general property of deep speech representations, by demonstrating its emergence in nine additional speech models covering both supervised and self-supervised. We then move beyond averaged word segments and show that in HuBERT, the circular trajectories are consistent enough at the level of individual words to perform word segmentation. Our approach, Rotary Segmentation (RoSeg), achieves 64.3% boundary F-score on Librispeech by detecting word boundaries when cycles complete in the temporal subspace. Although supervision is needed to identify a good subspace, nevertheless this result demonstrates much stronger implicit word knowledge in HuBERT than has previously been shown.

Machine Learning.title: Deep learning methods for gamma event selection in TAIGA-IACT image analysis in stereo-mode
Machine Learning.summary: In astrophysical complex TAIGA there are four Imaging Atmospheric Cherenkov telescopes (IACTs), located at a distance of 300-500 m from each other, due to which extensive air showers (EAS) generated by cosmic and gamma radiation are recorded by a single telescope or by multiple telescopes simultaneously (stereo-mode). The analysis of EAS images from two or more Cherenkov telescopes together is of particular interest, since for this approach the reconstruction of physical parameters of the primary gamma ray is much more accurate than in mono-observations. However, the gamma-ray event reconstruction strongly depends on the quality of the hadron background suppression of the classifier, therefore, the gamma event selection stage is one of the important ones in the further analysis of IACT data. We propose and study several neural network methods for gamma event selection in joint TAIGA-IACT image analysis. Neural network methods we suggested involves a single-stage analysis of IACT images from two telescopes, while the second method considers the formation of autoencoder-derived essential features that contain the EAS physical parameters, including the type of primary particle.
Machine Learning.comment: 10 pages, 4 figures, Proceedings of The 10th International Conference in Deep Learning in Computational Physics, July 6-8, 2026, Moscow, Russia

Machine Learning.title: Error Correction in Trained TTT Layers
Machine Learning.summary: Test-time-training (TTT) layers update fast-weight memory while processing an input sequence. A gradient-based update, however, does not by itself establish how the memory revises an existing association. We study the structure and empirical role of prediction-derived updates in released TTT implementations. For dot-product objectives, we characterize the absence of a prediction-error residual and establish conditions under which inner-loop ascent and descent are equivalent after reparameterization. For the LayerNorm-based squared-error objective used by TTT-Linear and TTT-MLP, we derive the inner gradient and identify a prediction-derived component that cancels at the released initialization in the zero-epsilon limit. We then measure the full normalized prediction's contribution on three trained checkpoints. Removing this contribution while retaining the LayerNorm Jacobian gives a mean gradient norm ratio of 0.25 to 0.32 across the models. On 100,303 tokens from War and Peace, the same intervention with local per-token norm matching raises perplexity by 2.8-2.9% on TTT-Linear-760M and 1.3B, whereas freezing all fast-weight updates raises it by factors of 4.2-4.5. Separate synthetic tests illustrate the dependence of plain delta-rule overwriting on step size. The results distinguish a prediction-derived update from its behavioral value and show why implementation analysis and live interventions are both needed to assess test-time memory.
Machine Learning.comment: 13 pages, 3 figures. Code and saved results included as ancillary material and at https://github.com/aliceyh7/ttt-error-correction

Machine Learning.title: SkillSpec: Consensus-Gated Agent Skill Evolution via Representation Specialization
Machine Learning.summary: Natural-language skills are textual procedural memories through which large language model (LLM) agents retain reusable task knowledge without updating model weights. Existing methods typically treat skills as either static artifacts or monolithic documents optimized using aggregate validation scores as feedback. However, representing a skill as a monolithic document restricts optimization to its textual content, without explicitly modeling the structure through which procedural knowledge is retrieved and executed. We identify a key distinction between learning what knowledge to retain and determining how to organize it: textual updates should first be validated through execution evidence, after which the retained knowledge should be structured according to its procedural dependencies and retrieval requirements. To this end, we introduce SkillSpec, a two-phase framework comprising consensus-gated evolution and representation specialization. In the consensus-gated phase, complementary editing intents generate complete candidate skills. An update is committed only when paired evaluations reach consensus, requiring sufficient overall improvement and non-negative aggregate paired gain in every repeated evaluation. In the specialization phase, signals of process and redundancy sensitivity derived from the full optimization trajectory, including accepted and rejected candidates, guide the selection of a flat, graph, or hybrid representation.Across six benchmarks and three target language models, SkillSpec improves average success rate over SkillOpt by 6.89%, averaged across the three models. These results demonstrate that reliable skill evolution and representation specialization address complementary objectives: deciding what knowledge to retain and how to structure it for inference.

Machine Learning.title: Flux-OPD: On-Policy Distillation with Evolving Contexts
Machine Learning.summary: Large language model training in open-ended domains lacks verifiable rewards, making task preferences difficult to formalize as effective supervision. Contexts derived from task feedback can provide richer supervision, yet fixed contexts cannot adapt as the student evolves, motivating contexts that evolve with student performance. However, directly using evolving contexts as in-training supervision results in unstable distillation targets and conflicting distributions, requiring mechanisms to stabilize the target and downweight conflicts. In this paper, we characterize context distillation through a reverse-KL decomposition, showing that the student is distilled toward the geometric mean of context-conditioned teachers, while the objective contains a conflict term measuring disagreement among these teachers. Motivated by this characterization, we propose Flux-OPD, an OPD paradigm that uses evolving contexts as in-training supervision to incorporate contextual signals derived from task feedback. Flux-OPD treats differences between context-conditioned and context-free teachers as contextual difference signals, injects them as contextual corrections into the context-free teacher, and weights the correction strength using the conflict term. Experiments show that Flux-OPD achieves the best results among OPD paradigms, highlighting the potential of combining teacher supervision with evolving contexts as in-training supervision.

Machine Learning.title: Spectral Considerations on Unsupervised Time-domain EEG Representation Learning with Deep Networks
Machine Learning.summary: Electroencephalography (EEG) is a non-invasive, scalable source of quantitative biomarkers for the early diagnosis of brain disorders, and deep representation learning has become a powerful paradigm for extracting information-rich latent features from raw signals. However, neural networks tend to under-represent high-frequency information, a concern that is especially acute for EEG given its oscillatory nature and characteristic $1/f^χ$ power decay, which risks masking disease-relevant high-frequency signatures. In this study, we systematically investigate the spectral constraints of unsupervised time-domain feature extraction across three autoencoder architectures (LSTMVAE, VAEEG, Transformer) and a state-of-the-art EEG foundation model. Using synthetic experiments and empirical validation, we show that while autoencoders capture macro-scale shifts such as alpha slowing, they remain biased against higher frequencies due to a magnitude-driven masking effect induced by the Mean Squared Error loss under 1/f-decaying spectra. Increasing latent dimensionality mitigates this attenuation but sacrifices latent compactness and generative stability. We argue that, as the field advances toward large-scale foundation-level feature extractors, it is imperative to move beyond simple time-domain reconstruction and to integrate spectral-domain loss terms and gradient-balancing techniques, so that the subtle high-frequency transients critical for diagnosing complex brain disorders are preserved in the latent representation.

Machine Learning.title: Hardware-Friendly Token-Group Activation Quantization for Low-Bit Mamba Super-Resolution
Machine Learning.summary: Mamba-based super-resolution models are efficient alternatives to Transformer-based restoration backbones, but their low-bit post-training quantization remains challenging because selective scan, Mamba's input-dependent state-space operator, induces different activation ranges across spatial tokens. Thus, a single layer-wise clipping range poorly matches all tokens. We propose Token-Group Quantization, a hardware-friendly activation PTQ framework that statically approximates a hardware-unfriendly post-scan grouping oracle, where tokens with similar preferred clipping ranges are assigned to the same group. To avoid runtime post-scan grouping in static low-bit inference, a lightweight predictor infers the groups from pre-scan features available before the quantized scan path. During calibration, we form pseudo-labels by clustering post-scan activation descriptors that capture similar rounding--clipping behavior. At inference, the frozen predictor maps pre-scan features to groups and selects entries from offline-calibrated group-wise clipping-bound tables, without runtime statistics collection, dynamic clipping updates, or post-scan group assignment. To address low-bit restoration degradation, we further introduce a Frequency-Preserving Refinement (FPR) objective for clipping-bound calibration. FPR aligns Fourier amplitude and phase between full-precision teacher and quantized student outputs to preserve high-frequency structures. Across PTQ protocols, bit-widths, backbones, and tasks, our method consistently outperforms prior Mamba and SR PTQ baselines, transfers to Transformer SR and Vision Mamba classification, composes with rotation-based quantization, and achieves 2.23x speedup on Jetson Orin Nano over FP16. Code is available here.
Machine Learning.comment: Accepted to NeurIPS 2026. 32 pages, 6 figures. Code: https://github.com/imaboybut/TGQ-MambaSR

Machine Learning.title: Flow Matching with Missing Data
Machine Learning.summary: Flow matching assumes fully observed training data, which many real-world applications rarely provide. We study Missing-Data Flow Matching, which treats the missing coordinates of training samples as latent variables and averages the flow matching loss over the values they could take. We first prove that the oracle correction is exact: completing from the true pattern-conditioned posterior recovers the complete-data flow-matching objective under any missingness mechanism. Under missing completely at random (MCAR) and missing at random (MAR), this posterior equals the ordinary complete-data conditional, while under missing not at random (MNAR) it generally depends on the missingness mechanism and may require additional structure to identify. Our finite-sample analysis then answers design questions that the algorithm leaves open. Missingness transfers estimator variance rather than adding it, and for the fixed-parameter loss estimator one completion per example matches complete-data variance and is optimal under a fixed evaluation budget. A learned completion model contributes population completion bias, which we bound by its expected conditional Wasserstein distance to the true completion law. Experiments numerically validate the theoretical predictions, show that deterministic rather than frozen imputation reduces generated conditional variability, and place our method alongside strong classical and deep imputation baselines on real tabular data.

Machine Learning.title: Discrete Flow Matching for Offline-to-Online Reinforcement Learning
Machine Learning.summary: Many reinforcement learning (RL) tasks have discrete action spaces, but most generative policy methods based on diffusion and flow matching are designed for continuous control. Meanwhile, generative policies usually rely heavily on offline datasets and offline-to online RL is itself challenging, as the policy must improve from new interaction without losing useful behavior learned from static data. To address those challenges, we introduce DRIFT, an online fine-tuning method that updates an offline pretrained continuous time Markov chain (CTMC) policy with an advantage-weighted discrete flow matching loss. To preserve useful pretrained knowledge, we add a path-space penalty that regularizes the full CTMC trajectory distribution, rather than only the final action distribution. For large discrete action spaces, we introduce a candidate-set approximation that updates the actor over a small subset of actions sampled from reference-policy rollouts and uniform exploration. Our theoretical analysis shows that focusing on a small set of high probability actions can reduce computation while keeping the approximation error small, making our method practical for large action spaces. We evaluate on macro-action MinAtar games where offline-pretrained DRIFT outperforms its online-only counterpart across all five games and achieves the highest mean return on three and on oracle free Jericho, DRIFT achieves a mean normalized score of 7.3\% with a lightweight GRU encoder, outperforming the evaluated pretrained language-model baselines. Ablations demonstrate the importance of appropriately weighted path-space regularization and reference-guided candidate construction.

Machine Learning.title: Reflected Proximal Dynamics for Accelerated High-Accuracy Log-Concave Sampling
Machine Learning.summary: We study sampling from $π(x)\propto\mathrm{e}^{-V(x)}$ on $\mathbb{R}^d$, where $V$ is $α$-strongly convex and $β$-smooth with condition number $κ=β/α$. For this problem, the proximal sampler preserves the target exactly and recovers overdamped Langevin dynamics in the small-step limit, but its Gaussian resampling step discards directional information. Underdamped Langevin dynamics retains such information through momentum to accelerate exploration, motivating a proximal construction that combines target preservation with directional persistence. We introduce \textit{reflected proximal dynamics}, which combines proximal sampling with an exact reflection of the auxiliary variable, conditional kinetic motion, and controlled refreshment. We develop two realizations: a flux-resampled underdamped half-turn and a persistent-momentum quarter-turn. From a warm start with constant $χ^2$ divergence, both methods achieve total variation error $\varepsilon$ using $\widetilde O(\sqrtκd^{1/4})$ expected oracle queries. We further remove the supplied warm-start assumption by combining either sampler with existing posterior samplers in a proximal initialization stage with an optimized coarse step size. Accounting for both initialization and sampling yields $\widetilde O(κ^{6/7}d^{1/4})$ expected oracle queries. In both regimes, the dependence on the target accuracy $\varepsilon$ is $\mathrm{polylog}(1/\varepsilon)$, making reflected proximal dynamics a promising framework for accelerated high-accuracy log-concave sampling.

Machine Learning.title: Towards Understanding Deep Learning Model in Image Recognition via Coverage Test
Machine Learning.summary: Deep neural networks (DNNs) play a crucial role in the field of artificial intelligence, and their security-related testing has been a prominent research focus. By inputting test cases, the behavior of models is examined for anomalies, and coverage metrics are utilized to determine the extent of neurons covered by these test cases. With the widespread application and advancement of DNNs, different types of neural behaviors have garnered attention, leading to the emergence of various coverage metrics for neural networks. However, there is currently a lack of empirical research on these coverage metrics, specifically in analyzing the relationships and patterns between model depth, configuration information, and neural network coverage. This paper aims to investigate the relationships and patterns of four coverage metrics: primary functionality, boundary, hierarchy, and structural coverage. A series of empirical experiments were conducted, selecting LeNet, VGG, and ResNet as different DNN architectures, along with 10 models of varying depths ranging from 5 to 54 layers, to compare and study the relationships between different depths, configuration information, and various neural network coverage metrics. Additionally, an investigation was carried out on the relationships between modified decision/condition coverage and dataset size. Finally, three potential future directions are proposed to further contribute to the security testing of DNN Models.

Machine Learning.title: Discrete MeanFlow: One-Step Generation via Conditional Transition Kernels
Machine Learning.summary: MeanFlow enables one-step generation in continuous spaces by learning an average velocity over a time interval rather than the instantaneous velocity field of flow matching. However, discrete state spaces lack smooth trajectories or spatial derivatives, so the continuous formulation does not directly apply. We introduce Discrete MeanFlow, a theoretical finite-state formulation that replaces point motion with probability-mass transport. Our key object is the conditional transition kernel of a continuous-time Markov chain (CTMC), from which we define a mean discrete rate that measures average transition-probability change over a finite interval. We prove a Discrete MeanFlow identity that relates this finite-interval rate to the instantaneous CTMC generator at the endpoint, using the Kolmogorov forward equation in place of the spatial chain rule in continuous MeanFlow. We parameterize the transition kernel directly using a boundary-by-construction design that guarantees valid probability outputs and exact boundary conditions without auxiliary losses. Because the learned kernel defines a probability distribution, generation requires only a single forward pass followed by direct sampling, eliminating the need for iterative denoising, ODE integration, or multi-step refinement. We validate the identity on exact finite-state Markov chains, demonstrating that the learned kernel recovers the analytical ground truth with high precision. We also investigate the training objective and the limits of factorization on synthetic sequence tasks across varying alphabet sizes and sequence lengths.

Machine Learning.title: Flow Matching for Offline Reinforcement Learning with Discrete Actions
Machine Learning.summary: Generative policies based on diffusion models and flow matching have shown strong promise for offline reinforcement learning (RL), but their applicability remains largely confined to continuous action spaces. To address a broader range of offline RL settings, we extend flow matching to a general framework that supports discrete action spaces with multiple objectives. Specifically, we replace continuous flows with continuous-time Markov chains, trained using a Q-weighted flow matching objective. We then extend our design to multi-agent settings, mitigating the exponential growth of joint action spaces via a factorized conditional path. We theoretically show that, under idealized conditions, optimizing this objective recovers the optimal policy. Extensive experiments further demonstrate that our method performs robustly across diverse settings and benchmarks, including high-dimensional control, multi-agent games, and dynamically changing preferences over multiple objectives, while outperforming traditional offline RL methods in practical multi-modal decision-making scenarios. Our discrete framework can also be applied to continuous-control problems through action quantization, providing a flexible trade-off between representational complexity and performance.

Machine Learning.title: From Simulated Fluids to Living Tissue: Zero-Shot Foundation Model Transfer to Perturbed Embryos
Machine Learning.summary:
Morphogenesis is driven by the interplay of genetic regulation and tissue mechanics. In vivo video data is limited, particularly under genetic mutations and environmental perturbations, making generalization beyond the most representative conditions in the dataset challenging. However, at tissue scales, the dynamics of Drosophila can be described as a continuum flow, motivating the usage of representations learned across other physical systems as priors for developmental dynamics.
  We investigate finetuning Walrus, a Continuum Dynamics Foundation Model pretrained across a broad set of simulated continuous systems, on tissue velocity fields from only 12 wild-type Drosophila blastoderm videos. We evaluate autoregressive prediction both in-distribution and zero-shot under unseen temperature and genetic perturbations. Zero-shot refers to evaluation on perturbation conditions never seen during wild-type finetuning, without any additional training. In-distribution, a Fourier Neural Operator model trained from scratch achieves best performance on VRMSE. However, Walrus (CRPS) is the strongest model under the most severe distribution shift of unseen samples of mutated embryos and temperature conditions. Interestingly, predictions capture the shape of the mean surface tissue velocity trajectory and its separation between 17°C and 27°C, including the timing of the peak at Germ Band Extension onset, a biologically meaningful milestone of embryo development.
  Our results provide preliminary support that representations learned from different dynamical systems can transfer to experimental morphogenesis in developmental regimes, provided they admit a continuum description. More broadly, our results motivate further study of physics foundation models as a new complementary tool for the simulation of morphogenesis in low-data regimes.

Machine Learning.title: Efficient Test-Time Adaptation through Latent Subspace Coefficients Search
Machine Learning.summary: Real-world deployment often exposes vision models to distribution shifts, making test-time adaptation (TTA) important for reliable prediction. Existing TTA methods can be difficult to deploy on edge devices because they require backpropagation, activation storage, or test-time batches, which increase computation, memory, and state. We propose \textbf{ELaTTA} (\textit{Efficient Latent Test-Time Adaptation}), a forward-only, gradient-free framework for single-instance TTA. ELaTTA freezes the pretrained model and adapts each test input by searching a low-dimensional coefficient vector in a principal latent subspace computed offline from a source-domain cache. The basis is stored once and source data are discarded before deployment. At test time, CMA-ES performs covariance-adaptive Gaussian search, ranks candidate corrections by prediction entropy, and selects the best candidate within a fixed evaluation budget. On five visual benchmarks spanning corruption, natural, rendition, sketch, and cross-domain shifts, ELaTTA provides strong accuracy under strict and continual single-instance protocols. In the strict single-instance comparison, MEMO requires \emph{64.7$\times$} the computation and \emph{12.4$\times$} the peak memory of ELaTTA. A complementary keyword-spotting experiment shows that the same coefficient-search design transfers beyond vision. We further demonstrate ViT-Base adaptation on a Raspberry Pi 5, confirming the feasibility of deploying ELaTTA on an edge device.

Machine Learning.title: AutoNovo: Agentic Program Search Discovers Transferable Nucleic Acid Design Algorithms
Machine Learning.summary: In-silico optimization of nucleic acids relies on predictive oracles that imperfectly capture biological function, so sequences optimized against one model may exploit model-specific artifacts and fail to generalize to independent models. Recent studies have shown that not all designers generalize equally well to independent models. In this work, we use agentic program search to iteratively propose, execute, evaluate, and revise code for nucleic-acid designers. We describe the successful strategies used to prompt the search. AutoNovo designers achieved the best observed mean among the evaluated methods on 3/3 DNA-design tasks in terms of in-silico performance, and 6/6 transfer tasks in terms of independent models. The designers come from a family of discovered nucleic acid designers rather than a single universal best designer. We plan to release the resulting designers. These results are the first steps in creating nucleic acid designers that maximize cross-model generalization, and thus improving the odds that in-silico designed sequences reflect real biology.
Machine Learning.comment: 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026). Workshop: Agentic AI for Biological Discovery

Machine Learning.title: NetRL: Powering Network Decisions via NetGRPO-Driven Reinforcement Learning
Machine Learning.summary:
Network decision-making tasks, including adaptive bitrate streaming, load balancing, and congestion control, require
  policies to process heterogeneous states and actions while balancing near- and long-term consequences. Existing solutions
  generalize poorly across network tasks, require substantial task-specific redesign, and lack reliable evaluation of long-
  horizon action consequences. Methods that learn through online interaction additionally face unstable optimization. We
  present NetRL, a two-stage LLM-based reinforcement learning framework that combines supervised fine-tuning on
  demonstration trajectories with online policy optimization. A universal mixed-embedding interface combines textual task
  descriptions with precise numerical states, while a network action head produces valid decisions. At its core, NetGRPO
  evaluates candidate actions over multiple future trajectories, directs deeper search toward uncertain alternatives
  through confidence-aware budgeting, and performs group-relative, clipped, and KL-regularized updates. NetRL achieves
  23.6% higher QoE than NetLLM, 12.2% lower job completion time than Genet, and 24.1% higher network utility than Orca,
  yielding state-of-the-art performance among the evaluated methods. Confidence-aware budgeting reduces end-to-end training
  time by 27.1% without reducing validation QoE. NetRL also converges stably and generalizes to unseen network traces
  without retraining. Code and model weights are available at the repository linked in this paper.

Machine Learning.title: When Participant Disjoint Validation Is Not Enough to Establish Generalization in Parkinson's Gait Classification
Machine Learning.summary: Participant-disjoint cross-validation prevents direct participant overlap, but it may still produce optimistic estimates when acquisition site and diagnosis are structurally dependent. We examined Parkinson's disease classification using 159 pressure-walkway summary features from 133 WearGait-PD participants, including 65 participants with Parkinson's disease and 68 controls. The cohort was non-factorial: two sites contained only one diagnostic group, whereas VA-Seattle was the only site containing both groups. In repeated participant-level nested cross-validation, site alone achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.955 plus or minus 0.003, exceeding the gait-feature model (0.882 plus or minus 0.014). Under the evaluated logistic-regression pipelines, adding gait features to site, age, and sex produced no measurable improvement in pooled discrimination. More site-controlled evaluations produced lower and imprecise estimates: VA-Seattle same-site AUC was 0.668 (95% bootstrap confidence interval 0.477 to 0.836), and the JHOC + Bayview-to-VA-Seattle transport stress test achieved 0.576 (0.375 to 0.770). Supporting within-diagnosis site-prediction and site-conditioned permutation analyses showed that the gait representation retained substantial acquisition-site structure. These findings indicate that participant-disjoint pooled validation did not isolate disease-related discrimination from site-associated variation. They encourage careful examination of site-label dependence and, where possible, support for pooled results through within-site or independent validation before broader claims are made about generalization across institutions.
Machine Learning.comment: 9 pages, 5 figures. Includes supplementary analyses integrated into the appendices

Machine Learning.title: Neural Non-Equilibrium Hamiltonian Monte Carlo for Corrected Boltzmann Sampling
Machine Learning.summary: Learned dynamical proposals can generate configurations without providing a tractable endpoint density. Nonequilibrium path probabilities offer a way to correct such proposals, but correction alone does not determine their ability to connect separated regions. We introduce Neural Non-Equilibrium Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (NHMC), which combines conditional momentum distributions with reversible, volume preserving dynamics. The forward--reverse path ratio gives the work used for training, importance weighting, normalizer estimation, and Metropolis correction. We then construct a configuration space round-trip kernel whose reverse and forward paths share an intermediate configuration. Conditional on that configuration, its path record update is independence Metropolis--Hastings. We compare its stationary inter-region flow with the flow obtained under exact conditional matching and bound their difference by the conditional path mismatch. This separates errors in the conditional proposal from dependence between the endpoint region and the intermediate configuration. Many well calculations test normalizers and mode probabilities; a controlled lattice $φ^4$ calculation compares ideal and accepted inter-sector flows and measures sector relaxation. In two dimensional $U(1)$, $\mathrm{SU}(2)$, and $\mathrm{SU}(3)$ gauge theories, corrected path weight estimates reproduce finite volume Wilson loops; $U(1)$ topological susceptibilities are also compared with analytic predictions across several lattice volumes.

Machine Learning.title: OneShot: Label-Efficient Detector Weighting for Time Series Anomaly Detection
Machine Learning.summary: Time series (TS) anomaly detection (AD) lacks a universal detector, with the best choice determined by the series rather than by the algorithm. Existing methods therefore either select one detector for each series or average a pool of them. However, both assume that no label ever arrives, while a deployed monitor does receive them, since an operator confirms the alarms it raises. In this paper, we propose ONESHOT, which uses a single confirmed anomaly to weight the pool rather than to choose one detector from it. Specifically, we score each detector on the confirmed anomaly, and those scores become the weights of a soft mixture over the whole pool. We show that a single confirmed anomaly is enough to come close to the best detector for the series. Across 152 univariate and 73 multivariate series, ONESHOT outperforms the strongest single detector, averaging the whole pool, and even picking the best detector on the confirmed event. Code is available at: https://github.com/seunghan96/one_shot.

Machine Learning.title: Accelerated Algorithm for Sparse Regularized Partial Optimal Transport
Machine Learning.summary: Partial Optimal Transport (POT) extends the classical optimal transport problem by relaxing the strict mass conservation constraint, enabling its use in a wide range of real-world applications. In many of these settings, sparse transport plans are preferred for their interpretability and computational benefits. While smooth and strongly convex regularizers - such as quadratic or elastic net - have been vastly used in various machine learning applications to induce sparsity and accelerate computation, they have received less algorithmic attention compared to entropic approaches for computational POT. In this paper, we propose a new optimization framework that leverages these regularizers through a penalty-based reformulation, enabling efficient gradient-based updates while preserving the structure of the original problem. Our method accommodates a broad class of regularizers that promote structured and sparse transport plans. Building on this formulation, we design an accelerated first-order algorithm that alternates between smooth updates and simple projection steps. Through empirical benchmarks on color transfer, domain adaptation, and point cloud registration, our approach consistently outperforms established baselines - achieving lower transport cost, higher sparsity, and faster convergence - making it a practical and scalable solution for modern transport problems.

Machine Learning.title: MP-MNCA: Morphology-Prior Masked Neighbor Cross-Attention for Efficient Spatial Domain Identification
Machine Learning.summary: Spatial transcriptomics jointly captures molecular state, tissue morphology, and spatial organization, yet spatial-domain methods are typically compared only at late training checkpoints, obscuring differences in convergence efficiency. We introduce MP-MNCA, a morphology-prior masked neighbor cross-attention framework that preserves the full 3,000 dimensional highly-variable-gene representation while selectively routing molecular information across spatial neighbors, with histological similarity incorporated as a continuous attention prior under a self-supervised masked neighbor-contrastive objective. Across 12 heterogeneous human dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) sections, MP-MNCA is evaluated against established spatial-domain baselines using both convergence trajectories and epoch-wise spatial-domain visualizations. Our results show that MP-MNCA (i) reaches coherent spatial-domain structure in substantially fewer training epochs, as reflected quantitatively by convergence curves and qualitatively by progressive spatial grids, and (ii) maintains strong clustering quality, achieving a mean peak refined ARI of 0.546 versus 0.549 for the strongest baseline (STAIG), while attaining the highest mean refined NMI of 0.657 versus 0.640. Moreover, MP-MNCA outperforms STAIG on 7 of 12 sections in ARI and 11 of 12 in NMI, demonstrating faster convergence without sacrificing spatial-domain quality.
Machine Learning.comment: Both authors contributed equally to this work

Machine Learning.title: GeoACE: Geometry-Diverse Anchor-Correction Ensembles for Heterogeneous Treatment Effect Estimation
Machine Learning.summary: Predicting heterogeneous causal effects supports informed decision-making, yet suitable inductive biases vary with treatment overlap, covariate imbalance, prognostic structure, and sample size. The Geometry-Diverse Anchor--Correction Expert Ensemble (GeoACE) addresses this variation through five complementary experts whose predictions are combined using weights estimated from validation data. Compared with ensemble designs that derive diversity primarily from sample or feature subsets, reweighting, or feature transformations, its central contribution is the coordinated design of training objectives and anchor geometries that target different prognostic and overlap structures. Following validation, each expert is refitted on the combined training and validation data, while retaining its distinctive structure. The shared architecture couples a structured outcome anchor with a learned neural correction. ACE serves as the reference estimator, while OW-ACE emphasizes well-supported covariate regions through overlap-weighted factual training. G$Φ$-ACE constructs a global outcome-guided geometry from pooled prognostic associations, whereas A$Φ$-ACE incorporates arm-specific outcome associations and penalties for treatment-group imbalance. O$Φ$-ACE complements these approaches with an outcome-free, overlap-aware projection that replaces the anchor input with a lower-dimensional representation. GeoACE is evaluated against 11 comparators on eight benchmark protocols, alongside comparisons of weighting rules and aggregation controls. It achieves the lowest mean $\sqrt{\mathrm{PEHE}}$ and absolute average treatment effect error on all three IHDP protocols and closely approaches the best comparator on NEWS, although performance varies across the remaining benchmarks. The aggregation analyses show similar observed performance for inverse-DR weighting and equal averaging.
Machine Learning.comment: 36 pages; 12-page supplementary material provided as an ancillary file. Revised title and exposition, expanded analyses, and clarified evaluation protocols

Machine Learning.title: MSC: Multi-Stage Caster-aware Control Framework with Uncertainty-Aware NMPC and RL-based Execution Layer
Machine Learning.summary: Freely swiveling casters are widely adopted in industrial AMRs/SDVs for their mechanical simplicity and load capacity. However, caster misalignment during low-speed or high-curvature maneuvers induces strong contact nonlinearities, widening the planning-execution gap between commanded $(v, ω)$ and realized motion. Existing caster-aware strategies are highly sensitive to state-estimation reliability, causing unstable execution in uncertain transition regimes. To address this, we present Multi-Stage Caster-aware Control (MSC), a planning-execution integrated hierarchical framework featuring two core mechanisms. First, an uncertainty-aware NMPC (CU-MPC) dynamically schedules caster-aware costs and input regularization using predictive uncertainty to suppress overly aggressive maneuvers. Second, a reinforcement learning-based execution layer estimates and predicts caster states under partial observability, transforming high-level velocity commands into physically executable wheel speeds adapted to current contact conditions. Validations in Isaac Sim and real robots demonstrate that MSC offers a clear comparative advantage over existing decoupled compensation approaches by significantly improving caster-state estimation accuracy, minimizing misalignment, and enhancing tracking robustness in caster-sensitive maneuvers.

Machine Learning.title: Exploration strategies for Gaussian process bandit optimization with inference regret guarantees
Machine Learning.summary: Existing cumulative regret guarantees for Bayesian optimization (BO) do not necessarily characterize the quality of the algorithm's final output. This gap is critical under noisy evaluations, where the goal is to return a single high-quality recommendation. To address it, we introduce efficient exploration strategies that can be incorporated into any BO procedure by occasionally replacing the acquisition query with an exploration query. To validate this approach, we bound the Gaussian process posterior standard deviation over the search space via the fill distance of the queries, which measures the largest region left unexplored. We then use this result to derive upper bounds on the inference regret, i.e., the gap between the global optimum and the function value at the algorithm's returned point. Empirically, these exploration strategies improve the final recommendations of existing BO algorithms on synthetic benchmarks, hyperparameter optimization, and a control task.

Machine Learning.title: Same Request, Different Answer: Quantization Amplifies Cache-Induced Divergence in LLM Serving
Machine Learning.summary: Major open-source serving stacks reuse the key-value tensors of a shared prefix by default. We measure what this prefix reuse costs in reproducibility. Holding model, decoding, seed and request order fixed at batch size one, we ran an eighty-episode multi-turn agentic tool-use workload with prefix reuse on and off across two engines and four weight formats. Without prefix reuse, repeated runs reproduced every token and log-probability in all ten configurations. With it, cache-hit and recompute paths diverged on both engines. On llama.cpp with GGUF weights this path divergence rises with quantization: for Qwen2.5-7B over ten independent server histories, it reached 37.4 percent of episodes at 16-bit and 82.5 percent at four-bit. Near-tie decisions became only about 1.2 times as common, while the cache-path change in top-two margins grew 4.9-fold from 16-bit to three-bit. Serving four-bit weights through 16-bit kernels left divergence not detectably different from 16-bit, placing the amplification mainly in the quantized execution path. At Q4_K_M, run-to-run divergence came mainly from llama.cpp's server-level prompt cache: under the canonical episode order it moved divergence by 37.5 points, and at its default, divergence spanned 20.0 to 28.7 percent under five random orders. With cache state restored, each path reproduced exactly while the two still differed. In the tested stacks, cached serving is irreproducible because the cache state is absent from the request and not reset by default. A single-turn bridge shows path divergence reaching task outcomes with no detectable net change in accuracy. We release the harness, logs, and analysis pipeline.
Machine Learning.comment: v2: revised after peer review at IEEE Access (resubmission under review). The main evidence is now a replicated controlled sweep: four weight formats, ten independent server histories, paired analyses. Adds restored-state, dequantization and latency controls. 19 pages, 3 figures, 7 tables. Code and data: https://github.com/aditi-p31/cache-divergence-study (tag resubmission-2026-10)

Machine Learning.title: Dependency Parsing Across the Resource Spectrum: Evaluating Architectures on High and Low-Resource Languages
Machine Learning.summary: Transformer-based models achieve state-of-the-art dependency parsing for high-resource languages, yet their advantage over simpler architectures in low-resource settings remains poorly understood. We evaluate four parsers---the Biaffine LSTM, Stack-Pointer Network, AfroXLMR-large, and RemBERT---across twelve typologically diverse languages, with a focus on low-resource African languages. We find that the Biaffine LSTM consistently outperforms transformer models in low-resource regimes, with transformers recovering their advantage as training data increases. The crossover falls within a resource range typical of treebanks for under-resourced languages. Morphological complexity (measured via MATTR) emerges as a significant secondary predictor of transformers' relative disadvantage after controlling for corpus size. These results indicate that the Biaffine LSTM may be better suited for syntactic tool development in low-resource regimes until sufficient annotated data is available to leverage the representational capacity of pre-trained transformers.
Machine Learning.comment: In Proceedings of the First International Conference on Language Technologies for Low-resource Languages (LaTeLL 2026)

Machine Learning.title: Error-Conditioned Neural Solvers
Machine Learning.summary: Neural surrogate models offer fast approximate mappings from PDE parameters to solutions, but they typically treat solving as a purely statistical task: once trained, they struggle to correct their own constraint violations and extrapolate beyond the training distribution. Recent hybrid methods promote physical correctness by targeting the PDE residual via gradient descent or Gauss--Newton steps, but inherit the compute cost and instability of the underlying classical optimizers. We show, theoretically and empirically, that numerically minimizing the PDE residual can be an unreliable proxy for reconstruction accuracy in ill-conditioned systems, explaining why these methods often do not make accurate predictions despite achieving low residuals. We propose error-conditioned Neural Solvers (ENS), built on a different principle: rather than an optimization target, the PDE residual field is passed as a direct input to the network at each iteration, enabling it to read the spatial structure of its own errors and learn an update policy to iteratively correct its predictions. Across four PDE families, ENS attains the highest prediction accuracy in the large majority of settings, with gains reaching $10\times$ on turbulent Kolmogorov flow, while avoiding the expensive compute cost of hybrid methods. ENS's learned correction policy generalizes under distribution shift, including zero-shot parameter changes and cross-equation transfer, where its relative advantage is largest in the ill-conditioned regimes where residual minimization is least reliable. Project website: https://neuralsolver.github.io/.

Machine Learning.title: Interactive 4D Volumetric Liquid Forecasting under Moving-Solid Interaction
Machine Learning.summary: We propose the task of Interactive 4D Volumetric Liquid Forecasting: predicting the spatiotemporal evolution of a future dense 3D liquid velocity field conditioned on how a solid object moves through it. This task provides an upstream physical forecasting primitive for systems that need to reason about motion-conditioned liquid response, including robotic liquid manipulation, digital twins, and rigid-fluid video generation. Existing works have made efforts in predicting flow around static or prescribed solid geometries and synthesizing visually plausible fluid motion. Yet these approaches provide limited coverage for interactive liquid dynamics, as they are not capable of forecasting how a moving solid induces a future full-domain liquid response. In this forecasting scenario, the hydrodynamic effect is condensed near an evolving liquid-solid interface, but the prediction target is a global spatiotemporal rollout. To address this challenge, we propose a two-level recurrent forecasting framework, TIDE/TIDES: TIDE isolates localized interface-driven forecasting, while TIDES adds transport-aware coupling and explicit stabilization to reduce accumulated rollout error. Across adapted neighboring baselines, controlled component ablations, motion/size OOD tests, and long-horizon evaluation, TIDES achieves the best forecasting performance and the ablations identify localized interaction, transport coupling, and stabilization as the key contributors. Together, our task formulation, benchmark, and TIDE/TIDES study establish a controlled foundation for moving-solid-conditioned dense liquid forecasting. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/jongwonryu/TIDE-TIDES.

Machine Learning.title: Auditing Finite-Lag Statistics of Recurrent Representations
Machine Learning.summary: Hidden-state trajectories are computational traces that record how recurrent representations evolve as networks process sequences. When exact state repeats are unavailable, one way to estimate conditional motion is to borrow successors from nearby states, yielding a finite-bandwidth successor smoother. However, this procedure can change the displacement being measured. At a median-distance bandwidth, write-phase displacement energy is about $1.88\times$ the exact value for GRU and LSTM. Elman instead shows near agreement in total energy despite large, opposing finite-bandwidth contributions. We therefore compute the conditional-mean energy fraction exactly on repeat-copy. Training reverses the architecture ordering of this fraction, with GRU and LSTM rising to about $94\%$ while Elman falls to about $55\%$. The centered remainder is small in energy but can still expose input information. For LSTM, linear four-bit decoding rises from $0.804$ on total displacement to $1.000$ after exact conditional centering.

Machine Learning.title: Think Before You Speak: Enabling Training-Free Latent Communication Between Language Models
Machine Learning.summary: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in solving complex tasks in coding, mathematical logic, and iterative reasoning, especially by coordinating effectively within multi-agent systems (MAS). However, language agents traditionally communicate via text exchange, which introduces a bottleneck in information transfer and adds prefill latency for downstream agents. Recent work proposes that directly sharing the key-value (KV) cache between language models can enable efficient latent collaboration, entirely bypassing standard text-based communication. To enable latent communication between heterogeneous models of different sizes, prior work introduces trained fusion adapters for each model pair, which limits practical deployment. We introduce CacheFuse, a training-free method which demonstrates that augmenting a downstream model with an upstream model's KV cache using linear interpolation consistently enables superior performance than the standalone downstream model can achieve. We systematically analyze CacheFuse across four reasoning and knowledge benchmarks and demonstrate up to 8.6 percentage points higher accuracy compared to single-model baselines and up to 12.2x TTFT speedup compared to text-based communication in multi-model inference.
Machine Learning.comment: Accepted at the 2nd Workshop on Efficient Reasoning at COLM 2026

Machine Learning.title: Fisher information and the geometry of memorization in neural networks
Machine Learning.summary: A fruitful approach towards understanding generalization in machine learning involves characterizing how models separate generalizable structure from idiosyncratic or even corrupted features of training data. Fisher information has emerged as a diagnostic tool for this separation, leveraging loss geometry to distinguish generalization from memorization. Here we investigate this connection in vision models trained on CIFAR-10 with controlled noise that can be learned only through memorization. We show that projecting model weights onto the top Fisher eigenvectors decouples general task performance from noisy sample memorization, and we investigate how this decoupling presents differentially across layers. We show that the same phenomena are present in small transformers trained to solve a synthetic in-context learning task, and are reproduced in closed form in a simple, analytically solvable linear model. Our results reveal that Fisher information captures aspects of the geometric structure underlying how neural networks allocate capacity between generalization and memorization.
Machine Learning.comment: 20 pages (10 pages main text), 11 figures (6 figures main text), NeurIPS 2026

Machine Learning.title: WildTrace: Evaluating Training Data Detection in Realistic Large-Scale LLM Post-Training
Machine Learning.summary: Although post-training significantly enhances model performance, the use of massive undisclosed data raises concerns about benchmark contamination and copyright infringement. This drives growing interest in training data detection for post-trained models. Existing evaluations for training data detection often leverage benchmarks constructed post hoc, which can introduce distribution shifts. Alternatively, controlled evaluations rely on small-scale training setups that diverge from realistic post-training settings. As a result, their reported performance may not faithfully reflect the effectiveness of detection methods in real-world scenarios. To this end, we introduce \textsc{\method}, a reliable benchmark designed to evaluate detection methods in realistic, large-scale post-training settings. Built on a multi-stage pipeline, \method\space encompasses stage-specific models throughout the post-training lifecycle, spanning SFT, DPO, and RL. To perform a reliable evaluation, we construct model-specific evaluation sets across four diverse tasks, featuring distribution-matched members and non-members with verifiable membership labels. Our results reveal that even the best-performing method achieves an average AUC of only 0.529 on our benchmark, which approaches random-guessing level (0.5). Furthermore, our analysis suggests that evaluation protocols can significantly affect measured detection performance. These findings highlight the significant potential for developing effective, practical, and robust detection methods under realistic scenarios.

Machine Learning.title: Do LLMs Learn from Rewards in Context? : Rethinking the role of reward in In-Context RL
Machine Learning.summary: LLM agents increasingly improve at inference time by accumulating experience in context rather than by updating parameters. This process is often described as in-context reinforcement learning (ICRL). Whether in-context learning (ICL) can actually play the role of RL, however, has not been tested. We study this question in its simplest form, direct ICRL, where the model conditions directly on raw trajectory-reward pairs, and ask whether the reward acts as a learning signal. Through controlled experiments on four benchmarks across six models, we find that the reward is read, but its effect is small: flipping, randomizing, or removing the reward leaves the improvement curve almost unchanged, and this holds even under meta-prompts that explicitly instruct the model to explore, exploit, or reason over rewards. Trajectories drive improvement, but not through their semantic content: shuffled or corrupted trajectories work as well as real ones. These patterns closely mirror those known in ICL, suggesting that direct ICRL is better understood as a special case of ICL than as inference-time RL. This reframing has implications for agent memory design: ICL factors such as input distribution and demonstrations may matter more than RL elements such as reward shaping and exploration.

Machine Learning.title: Equilibrium Learning in Unbounded Stochastic Games with Gaussian Transitions
Machine Learning.summary: Learning equilibria from data is difficult when several decision makers interact indefinitely and the system state has no prescribed bounds. We examine discounted general-sum stochastic games with compact action sets and an unknown nonlinear drift observed through Gaussian transition noise. The proposed procedure uses a single uninterrupted trajectory to update Gaussian-process models of the drift and to solve successively refined finite games. We prove a perturbation result showing that stability of equilibrium selection, together with uniform KL accuracy of Gaussian transition models, is sufficient for regional uniform convergence of the induced values and approximate Nash behavior in the original game. The region specifies where the guarantees are evaluated; strategies and dynamics continue to act on the entire Euclidean state space. For GP estimators, simultaneous confidence bounds yield a rate controlled by posterior uncertainty, kernel information gain, and joint-state dimension. Numerical studies illustrate how kernel choice and dimension appear in the predicted convergence behavior.

Machine Learning.title: PACEvolve++: Improving Test-time Learning for Evolutionary Search Agents
Machine Learning.summary: Large language models have become drivers of evolutionary search, but most systems rely on a fixed, prompt-elicited policy to sample next candidates. This limits adaptation in practical engineering and research tasks, where evaluations are expensive, and progress depends on learning task-specific search dynamics. We introduce PACEvolve++, an advisor-model reinforcement learning framework for test-time policy adaptation in evolutionary search agents. PACEvolve++ decouples strategic search decisions from implementation: a trainable advisor generates, assesses, and selects hypotheses, while a stronger frontier model translates selected hypotheses into executable candidates. To train the advisor under non-stationary feedback, we propose a phase-adaptive approach that adapts its optimization strategy to different phases of the evolutionary process. Early in evolution, it uses group-relative feedback to learn broad search preferences; later, as reward gaps compress, it emphasizes best-of-$k$ frontier contribution to support stable refinement. Across expert-parallel load balancing, sequential recommendation, and protein fitness extrapolation, PACEvolve++ outperforms the state-of-the-art evolutionary search framework with frontier models, achieving faster convergence and stabilizing test-time training during evolutionary search.

Machine Learning.title: BARTER: Compact Dynamic Sparse Training with Standard Dense Kernels
Machine Learning.summary: Dynamic sparse training (DST) aims to reduce training costs while maintaining accuracy. Existing DST methods mask out parameters but keep matrix dimensions unchanged. Training speedups therefore depend on specialized support, such as sparse kernels. We introduce BARTER, a structured DST framework that reduces training cost using standard dense kernels by keeping training tensors physically compact while dynamically reallocating capacity across layers. Unlike existing works that require computing gradients for all parameters, BARTER instead uses statistics collected only from active units during ordinary backpropagation to prune and clone attention heads and feed-forward channels under separate fixed global budgets. At each topology update, it resizes the affected parameter tensors and remaps their optimizer states, so subsequent training steps operate directly on the compact model. Training and fine-tuning experiments with Transformer-based vision models on two image classification benchmarks at densities from $0.1$ to $0.7$ show competitive Top-1 accuracy relative to full-tensor DST baselines. On an NVIDIA L40, BARTER achieves speedups of up to $6.29\times$ in measured training segments and reduces peak allocated GPU memory by up to $81.3\%$ relative to these implementations. An iPhone 13 Pro Max training benchmark additionally shows a $2.78\times$ speedup over the full-tensor DST baseline.

Machine Learning.title: Sera: Semantic Representation Aggregation with Knowledge and LLM for Reliable and Interpretable Battery Health Forecasting
Machine Learning.summary: Battery state of health (SoH) forecasting is important for battery management, but remains challenging due to nonlinear degradation and heterogeneity across batteries. Existing data-driven approaches primarily use temporal models to learn from numerical battery time series, and higher-level degradation characteristics are often not explicitly represented. These characteristics, however, can provide degradation guidance to support reliable forecasting and make the influence of degradation more interpretable. In this paper, we propose Sera, a semantic representation aggregation framework that complements temporal modelling with degradation semantics. Guided by battery domain expertise, Sera extracts degradation semantics from time series and constructs two complementary representations using rule-based knowledge and LLM-based interpretation. The representations are independently encoded and integrated with the representation learned by temporal models through gated aggregations. Experiments on the mainstream benchmark across multiple prediction horizons and different temporal models show that Sera consistently improves forecasting performance, achieving up to a 37.3% reduction in prediction error over the temporal baseline and enhanced generalizability. Counterfactual analysis examines how forecasts respond to changes in degradation semantics to assess interpretability. The results show that prediction responses are consistent with the meanings of key degradation descriptors across tested horizons. Together, these findings demonstrate that structured degradation semantics and effective aggregation can improve forecasting accuracy and support reliable and interpretable battery health forecasting for advanced battery management.

Machine Learning.title: Distributional Regression for Arbitrary Response Variables Using ReLU Neural Networks
Machine Learning.summary: This paper develops a unified framework for distributional regression with arbitrary response variables. Rather than relying on scalar thresholds or Euclidean structure, we model conditional event probabilities indexed by measurable sets, which extends distributional regression to general response spaces while retaining a direct connection to classical event-based formulations. Within this framework, we study two complementary estimators: a preliminary estimator based on separate regression of event indicators, and a constrained estimator that enforces inclusion-consistent predictions through a directed acyclic graph (DAG) over a finite set family. We establish general error bounds for both estimators and further specialize the results to dense ReLU networks, yielding explicit convergence rates overcoming the curse of dimensionality. Simulation studies and real-data experiments further demonstrate the practical effectiveness of the proposed framework.

Machine Learning.title: XForecast: The KDD 2026 Finance Day Challenge on News-Grounded Financial Forecasting
Machine Learning.summary: Financial forecasting has traditionally relied on numerical time-series (TS) signals, while textual information such as news remains largely underutilized. We introduce XForecast, a benchmark and competition for news-grounded financial forecasting, where the task is to predict stock price movements four weeks ahead using both historical price data and paired news signals. XForecast combines stock price data with curated financial text generated using FinTexTS, a multimodal dataset generation method. It covers 100 large-cap stocks from 2019--2023, with training on 2019--2022 and evaluation on 2023. To better evaluate models that leverage textual signals, we adopt a weighted hit rate metric that places greater emphasis on instances where news information is expected to have stronger influence. The XForecast Challenge, hosted on Kaggle as part of KDD 2026 Finance Day, aims to benchmark methods for integrating financial TS and textual information.

Machine Learning.title: PID-Gated Continual Prompt Adaptation Under Noisy Feedback
Machine Learning.summary: Deploying LLM agents in non-stationary environments requires continually revising their instructions as the task drifts, yet rewriting after every reported mistake can turn noisy feedback into persistent errors. This raises an often-overlooked scheduling question in prompt adaptation: when should feedback trigger a lasting instruction update, and at what editor-call cost? Taking inspiration from proportional-integral-derivative (PID) control, we introduce a family of lightweight gates that react to the current error, accumulate evidence over time, and roll back deterioration after an edit. We benchmark these gates against both simple baselines and advanced prompt optimizers (TextGrad and GEPA), over a diverse suite of drifting tasks, LLM parameter sizes, feedback-noise levels, and random seeds. PID-gated continual prompt adaptation yields a more favorable Pareto trade-off between task performance (high accuracy, low error) and editor-call budget than the baselines considered, pointing to control-theoretic scheduling as a simple, general tool for robust prompt adaptation under unreliable feedback.

Machine Learning.title: Optimal Diagonal Preconditioning Beyond Worst-Case Conditioning: Theory and Practice of Omega Scaling
Machine Learning.summary:
We study optimal diagonal preconditioning using the classical worst-case $κ$-condition number and the averaging-based $ω$-condition number.
  For the $κ$-optimal preconditioning problem, we derive an affine-based pseudoconvex reformulation with three key advantages: all stationary points are global minima, subgradients are inexpensive to compute, and the optimization variable is an $n$-dimensional vector rather than an $n\times n$ matrix as in semidefinite programming (SDP) approaches. We develop a simple and highly efficient subgradient method, with convergence guarantees, for solving this pseudoconvex formulation that is substantially more scalable and accurate than existing SDP-based methods.
  For the $ω$-condition number, we provide explicit characterizations of optimal diagonal and block diagonal preconditioners. In particular, we show that several classical preconditioners, including Jacobi and row/column normalization, are $ω$-optimal, and that matrix balancing schemes monotonically reduce $ω$ and converge to stationary points of the two-sided problem. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first unified and explicit characterization of optimality conditions for both $κ$ and $ω$-based preconditioning.
  Our numerical experiments further reveal a striking phenomenon: although $κ$-optimal preconditioners achieve stronger reductions in the worst-case condition number, $ω$-optimal preconditioners are substantially cheaper to compute and yield better performance for iterative methods such as preconditioned conjugate gradient (PCG) and least squares method (LSQR). Moreover, applying $ω$-optimal scaling to linear systems that are already $κ$-optimally preconditioned leads to further improvements in PCG iterations.

Machine Learning.title: Beyond GRPO and On-Policy Distillation: An Empirical Sparse-to-Dense Reward Principle for Language-Model Post-Training
Machine Learning.summary: In settings where labeled verifiable training data is the binding constraint, each checked example should be allocated to the model and reward density where it is most informative. We identify a reward-density principle: sparse sequence-level reward is most useful on models that can explore and discover better behavior, while dense token-level teacher supervision is better suited for compressing that behavior into a smaller deployment model; accordingly, scarce labeled data should be used upstream on the strongest available teacher, then transferred downstream as dense supervision. We evaluate this rule through a four-stage workflow:teacher RL, forward-KL warmup, on-policy distillation, optional post-bridge student RL on verifiable math and code generation with Qwen3, Llama, and Qwen2.5 models. At fixed Qwen3-1.7B deployment-student size, an RL-improved 8B teacher distilled through the dense bridge outperforms direct GRPO on the same student ($79.3\%$ vs.\ $75.9\%$ on MATH; $25.2\%$ vs.\ $19.8\%$ on AIME~2024), while transfer from the same teacher before RL underperforms. A component ablation confirms that each stage is load-bearing: the RL-improved teacher adds $7.8$ absolute points on MATH over a raw teacher of the same size, the forward-KL warmup adds $1.7$, and on-policy distillation adds $3.3$. The teacher-quality ordering: raw-teacher transfer $<$ direct GRPO $<$ RL-teacher transfer, replicates on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct with a Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct teacher and on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct for code generation with a Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct teacher. The operational lesson is to avoid spending scarce labeled data on the least prepared policy: use sparse reward for teacher-side discovery, dense transfer for student compression, and student-side sparse reward only after the bridge. The OPD implementation used in our experiments is available at https://github.com/HJSang/OPSD_OnPolicyDistillation.

Machine Learning.title: Elephant in the Fridge: Constant-Memory Frame Packing for Long Video Understanding
Machine Learning.summary: Hour-long videos, streaming feeds, and movie-length content are pushing vision-language models (VLMs) past their breaking point -- the standard recipe of encoding each frame into visual tokens yields sequences that grow linearly with video length, causing prohibitive memory consumption and inference latency. Existing approaches, such as token reduction and keyframe selection, shorten the token sequence but leave the O(n) scaling intact, failing to resolve the fundamental bottleneck. We propose FramePack-U, a strikingly simple, training-free frame packing framework that compresses arbitrarily long videos into a fixed size visual representation at constant memory cost. FramePack-U requires no fine-tuning or architectural modification -- it plugs directly into off-the-shelf VLMs at inference time. Inspired by FramePack from the generation literature, we propose a content-aware compression strategy for visual understanding under a fixed token budget. Specifically, FramePack-U (1) scores each frame by its semantic similarity to the text prompt and ranks frames in a diversity-driven manner, and (2) packs the selected frames at varying resolutions into a fixed-length context window. This concentrates the memory budget on frames that are both instruction-relevant and visually diverse. While FramePack-U can in theory pack arbitrarily many frames into the fixed budget, we identify an empirical instantiation that generalizes robustly across settings. Extensive experiments on LongVideoBench, MLVU, and Video-MME show that FramePack-U consistently outperforms full-resolution baselines and prior token reduction and keyframe selection methods across diverse model families, parameter scales, and frame budgets. Notably, on Qwen3.5-35B-A3B with a 128-frame budget, FramePack-U yields gains of +12.9\%, +10.6\%, and +9.7\% over the official model on the three benchmarks, respectively.

Machine Learning.title: Stochastic Grouping Conformal Prediction for Effective Subgroup Reliability
