Machine Learning.summary: Conformal prediction offers a distribution-free coverage guarantee, making it especially attractive for clinical applications. Standard conformal prediction, however, provides such guarantees only at the population level, and its prediction sets can exhibit coverage disparities across clinically important subgroups. A natural remedy is to calibrate within predefined groups. However, this can require access to sensitive subgroup attributes and is prone to a worst-group bottleneck: protecting the most difficult subgroup can inflate prediction sets for all, increasing cognitive burden on decision makers. To this end, we propose Stochastic Grouping Conformal Prediction (SGCP), a conformal framework for subgroup-reliable uncertainty quantification. It learns a stochastic grouping map that allows each sample to draw calibration information from others with similar calibration behavior, yielding a local score law that boosts reliability across subpopulations. We prove that SGCP retains the standard coverage guarantee. Experiments on synthetic and real-world benchmarks show that it consistently reduces subgroup coverage gaps while achieving smaller or comparable prediction set sizes relative to existing baselines.

Machine Learning.title: Golden Anchor for Video Generation
Machine Learning.summary: Video generation supports digital content creation, with applications in virtual avatars, AI-driven filmmaking, interactive game engines, and world models. State-of-the-art systems achieve controllability primarily through image-to-video (I2V) generation, in which an injected anchor image determines the identity, composition, and style of the resulting video. In modern pipelines, this anchor is synthesized by a text-to-image (T2I) generator. This raises a largely overlooked question: Are images obtained directly from the T2I model truly suitable for current video models? Our analysis shows that anchor aesthetic and quality scores are weakly correlated with downstream video quality. The structure-and-texture score is negatively correlated with I2V video quality in both the visual and motion dimensions. Fine-tuning the T2I model on an image reward accordingly yields anchors with visibly denser structural and character detail: they score higher on image metrics, yet lower the video reward on every I2V model we test and change downstream motion unpredictably. We therefore introduce Golden Anchor Learning (GAL), to our knowledge the first framework for learning golden anchors by optimizing a T2I generator with downstream video feedback. GAL evaluates candidate anchors through the videos they induce under a frozen I2V model and converts video rewards into image-level preferences for DPO fine-tuning of the T2I generator. On all four I2V models, GAL raises the VBench average by $2.97\%$--$8.46\%$ over the untuned generator. The rendered clips also score higher under VideoReward-Overall, and their extracted frames under HPSv3 and UniPercept. GAL yields consistent motion gains across all four I2V models, as measured by a $5.62\%$--$38.24\%$ increase in VBench dynamic degree. Although GAL is trained only on HunyuanVideo-1.5 renders, these gains extend to the other three I2V models.
Machine Learning.comment: 22 pages (including references and appendices), 3 figures, 8 tables

Machine Learning.title: Silence and Noise: Resolving Suppression and Overvaluation in Multimodal Entity Alignment
Machine Learning.summary: Multimodal entity alignment (MMEA) is fundamental to integrating heterogeneous knowledge graphs (KGs), yet existing paradigms remain critically vulnerable to incomplete modalities and cross-graph structural asymmetries. This paper exposes a fundamental oversight in current MMEA research: treating feature missingness and topological discrepancies as isolated preprocessing or denoising challenges, which overlooks their destructive coupling during multimodal fusion. We systematically formulate and evaluate two newly identified failure modes: 1) Detail Missing (DM)-induced overvaluation, where the absence of local modality details causes models to overemphasize uninformative, blurred representations; and 2) Context Imbalance (CI)-induced suppression, where topological discrepancies across KGs allow dense structural contexts to overwhelm weaker but highly discriminative modal signals, triggering high-level semantic drift. To break this cycle of degradation, we introduce ALMEA, a generative and calibration framework that establishes a bidirectional feedback loop between low-level feature reconstruction and high-level latent space alignment. Specifically, Cross-Modality Imputation (CMI) synthesizes missing modality details to mitigate overvaluation, while Latent Semantic Calibration (LSC) aligns cross-graph joint embeddings to suppress topology-driven semantic drift. Under sparse supervision, we develop Controlled Iterative Selection (CIS) to adaptively acquire representative and diverse pseudo-labeled pairs, optimizing latent calibration under constrained budgets. Extensive evaluations on standard benchmarks demonstrate that ALMEA consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. At a 20% supervision rate, ALMEA yields substantial absolute improvements of up to 5.20% in MRR and 6.40% in Hits@1, maintaining robust gains across higher supervision thresholds.

Machine Learning.title: Beyond Policy Rollouts: Embedding-Space Directional Exploration with Anchored Noise for LLM RLVR
Machine Learning.summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) typically uses small rollout groups per prompt, where repeated sampling from the same policy can yield highly similar trajectories, reducing within-group reward variation and weakening group-relative advantage signals. Existing remedies such as higher sampling temperature, entropy bonuses, asymmetric clipping, and larger rollout budgets broaden sampling or modify policy updates but leave rollout conditioning unchanged. In this paper, we propose EDEN (Embedding-space Directional Exploration via anchored Noise), which intervenes at the rollout source through anchored input perturbations. EDEN explores beyond the policy's own rollouts. Within the same rollout budget, it replaces a small fraction of standard rollouts in each group with rollouts that the same policy generates from the prompt plus a single appended, perturbed embedding position, rather than from the prompt alone. Gaussian noise drives variation, while a shared anchor provides a common conditioning direction within each prompt group. Selected perturbed rollouts contribute to GRPO updates with downweighted advantages, and the model architecture, discrete decoding, and test-time inference remain unchanged. Across model scales and mathematical reasoning benchmarks, EDEN outperforms GRPO and the exploration controls evaluated in the same pipeline, with the largest gains in sampled solution coverage. Analyses show that more prompt groups provide non-zero group-relative learning signals and that noise and anchoring play complementary roles. Intervening at the rollout source is thus an effective lever for exploration in RLVR.

Machine Learning.title: SelectTTRL: Representation-Guided Data Selection for Efficient Test-Time Reinforcement Learning
Machine Learning.summary: Test-Time Reinforcement Learning (TTRL) enables large language models to adapt directly on unlabeled test problems by constructing pseudo-labels from multiple sampled responses. However, existing TTRL methods typically apply the same expensive sampling and optimization procedure to all test problems, despite substantial differences in their training utility. In this paper, we study whether such problems can be identified before costly test-time training, without access to ground-truth answers. We uncover a stable relationship between internal response representations and problem-level empirical accuracy. Specifically, we define COS as the cosine similarity between a model's response representation and a correctness-related direction constructed from an independent question-answering dataset. COS consistently correlates with problem solvability across different models, datasets, and experimental settings, and we further provide a theoretical analysis explaining this relationship. Building on this finding, we propose SelectTTRL, a representation-guided data selection method that ranks test problems using COS and applies TTRL only to a selected percentile interval. SelectTTRL leaves the standard TTRL pipeline unchanged for the selected problems, while avoiding unnecessary multi-response sampling and reinforcement learning updates on the remaining ones. Experiments across multiple reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that SelectTTRL substantially reduces test-time computation while maintaining or improving the performance of standard TTRL. Code is available at https://github.com/heyiliyi/SelectTTRL-public.

Machine Learning.title: CloneOT: predicting clone-specific perturbation responses with lineage-supervised neural inverse optimal transport
Machine Learning.summary: Predicting single-cell perturbation responses requires mapping between two unpaired populations of cells measured before and after the perturbation. Optimal transport (OT) provides a principled framework for constructing such mappings by minimizing the transport cost, and neural OT methods (\textit{e.g.}, CellOT) have been employed for this prediction task. However, these methods rely on a fixed transport cost, typically the squared Euclidean distance. This cost may connect cells with the wrong responses. Lineage tracing provides the information needed to learn the cost, as heritable barcodes link the cells of the same clone before and after the perturbation. Here, we propose \CloneOT, a neural inverse OT method that learns both the transport cost and the transport map from partially lineage-traced single-cell datasets. \CloneOT\ represents the cost as a neural network. It learns the cost by minimizing the extra cost that the lineage adds to the optimal transport, so that the cheapest transport keeps the cells of each clone together. Our experiments demonstrate that \CloneOT\ recovers the correct transport on 2D datasets, while the squared Euclidean cost fails. Moreover, \CloneOT\ outperforms five baselines on 14 lineage-tracing perturbation scenarios of cancer cells, for both seen and unseen clones. Furthermore, we show that \CloneOT\ reveals the clone-specific transcriptional programs of drug-tolerant persister cells and forecasts the fate of each clone from its cells before treatment. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/poseidonchan/CloneOT.

Machine Learning.title: Self-Creating Random Walks for Decentralized Learning under Pac-Man Attacks
Machine Learning.summary: Random walk (RW)-based algorithms have long been popular in distributed systems due to low overheads and scalability, with recent growing applications in decentralized learning. However, their reliance on local interactions makes them inherently vulnerable to malicious behavior. In this work, we investigate an adversarial threat that we term the ``Pac-Man'' attack, in which a malicious node probabilistically terminates any RW that visits it. This stealthy behavior gradually eliminates active RWs from the network, effectively halting the learning process without triggering failure alarms. To counter this threat, we propose the CREATE-IF-LATE (CIL) algorithm, which is a fully decentralized, resilient mechanism that enables self-creating RWs and prevents RW extinction in the presence of Pac-Man. Our theoretical analysis shows that the CIL algorithm guarantees several desirable properties, such as (i) non-extinction of the RW population, (ii) almost sure boundedness of the RW population, and (iii) convergence of RW-based stochastic gradient descent even in the presence of Pac-Man with a quantifiable deviation from the true optimum. Moreover, the learning process experiences at most a linear time delay due to Pac-Man interruptions and RW regeneration. Our extensive empirical results on both synthetic and public benchmark datasets validate our theoretical findings.
Machine Learning.comment: arXiv admin note: substantial text overlap with arXiv:2508.05663

Machine Learning.title: Memorization in image classification: test set behavior and scaling laws
Machine Learning.summary: Deep neural networks are capable of both learning generalizing solutions on natural tasks and memorizing arbitrary mappings. We argue that understanding the former requires understanding the latter, which is much less studied. In what ways do networks that generalize or memorize differ in their behavior or their training dynamics? Do memorizing networks simply function as a lookup table where input-output mappings are stored independently? We investigate these questions in the context of CNNs trained on image classification tasks with randomized labels or pixels. We first study the behavior of such memorizing networks on unseen images. We find that independently initialized networks trained on the same random labels learn different predictive functions: they make different predictions on test examples, in contrast with generalizing networks. We then examine the effect of dataset size on memorization through the required network capacity and training time to interpolate the training set. Counter-intuitively, we find that the number of presentations of a given example required for complete memorization can decrease with dataset size even when input-output pairs share no common structure. Although memorizing networks do not learn a universal solution, they exhibit interesting behaviors which call for further investigations into the underlying mechanisms.
Machine Learning.comment: 11 Pages, 4 figures, Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Neural Network Artifacts as a New Data Modality

Machine Learning.title: ReLoop: Structured Modeling and Behavioral Verification for Reliable LLM-Based Optimization
Machine Learning.summary: Large language models (LLMs) can translate natural-language problem descriptions into optimization code, but the code is prone to silent failures: it executes and returns a solver-feasible solution while encoding a semantically incorrect formulation. On compositional problems, the resulting feasibility-correctness gap reaches 90 percentage points. We introduce ReLoop, which combines two mechanisms. Structured generation decomposes code production into a four-stage reasoning chain (understand, formalize, synthesize, verify) to reduce formulation errors during generation. Behavioral verification detects the errors that remain by testing whether the formulation responds correctly to solver-based parameter perturbation, a signal that comes from the solver rather than from LLM self-review and requires no ground truth. The two mechanisms address different error structures: structured generation gives the largest gain on compositional problems (+8.5pp accuracy on RetailOpt-190 with Claude Opus 4.6), and behavioral verification gives its largest gain on localized defects (+4.4pp on MAMO-ComplexLP). With diagnostic execution recovery, ReLoop reaches 100% executable code on Claude Opus 4.6, and relative to direct generation it raises or preserves every reported metric of the three chat-tuned foundation models on all three benchmarks. For the narrowly fine-tuned SFT model we test, the chain-of-thought prompt conflicts with its learned output format and lowers its accuracy on MAMO-ComplexLP; we document and analyze this interaction. We release RetailOpt-190, 190 compositional retail optimization scenarios in which several constraints interact.

Machine Learning.title: Regime-Aware Router Learning for Multi-Domain Medical Image Generation with Diffusion Experts
Machine Learning.summary: Heterogeneous medical image data motivate domain-specialized diffusion experts, but expert specialization alone does not determine how their predictions should be combined during sampling. Learning a global router is particularly challenging when the server has limited, potentially unrepresentative images. We study two router-learning strategies for a fixed expert pool. Server-Only learns input- and timestep-dependent expert assignments from server images with component labels. Anchor-Delta (AD) uses the same images and frozen experts to obtain additional evidence from denoising losses. It distills targets that combine this evidence with the current router's assignments, while a proxy gate controls a subsequent refinement step. Component labels describe data origin; expert losses measure empirical prediction performance. We evaluate these distinct signals through routing analyses and paired medical image generation. An AD-trained router improves generation metrics over Server-Only in a heterogeneous four-domain setting, and a separate server-data study shows gains in held-out routing over a corrected-routing comparator. Additional paired evaluations show that the effect of inference-time evidence mixing varies across benchmarks. These findings establish server-data availability and expert performance as distinct considerations in learning routers for multi-domain diffusion models.

Machine Learning.title: Beyond Single-Pathogen Forecasts: Predicting Shared Respiratory Hospital Burden from Influenza, COVID-19, and RSV
Machine Learning.summary: Co-circulating influenza, COVID-19, and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) create a shared hospital-admission burden, because beds, staff, testing capacity, and respiratory support are allocated to total demand rather than to one pathogen at a time. This makes respiratory forecasting a target-construction problem as well as a modeling problem: disease-specific forecasts preserve attribution, whereas hospitals also need a single planning signal for combined burden. We developed a supervised 1- to 4-week-ahead framework for weekly admissions and compared two total-burden strategies: summing independently generated pathogen-specific forecasts and forecasting the combined admission target directly. Evaluation included retrospective held-out testing and prospective operational forecasts issued before the corresponding admission weeks were observed, with performance summarized using MAE and Percent Agreement (PA; the smaller of model-generated and observed counts divided by the larger). In retrospective total-burden evaluation, the combined-burden model had PA values of 0.85, 0.78, 0.74, and 0.76 and MAE values of 80.63, 200.09, 183.97, and 156.13 from week 1 to week 4 ahead, compared with summed-forecast PA values of 0.85, 0.80, 0.69, and 0.69 and MAE values of 100.14, 200.06, 205.65, and 217.57. Prospectively, the combined-burden model had higher PA and lower MAE at all four horizons, with the largest separations at weeks 3 and 4 ahead. These results support layered respiratory forecasting: pathogen-specific forecasts remain necessary for etiologic interpretation, while combined-burden forecasts better align with hospital preparedness and shared-capacity planning.

Machine Learning.title: Why Learning Rediscovers the Closed-Form Diagonal Regularizer
Machine Learning.summary: Recovering modal amplitudes from a few sensors requires regularization, and the shape of the penalty decides how strongly each mode is shrunk. The best shape depends on the truncation noise that discarded modes add to every measurement, which is unobserved and could be room-specific. We identify a diagonal saturation principle: for a single snapshot, isotropic truncation noise makes the Bayes-optimal Tikhonov shape a closed-form power law Gamma_k proportional to lambda_k^|s|, set by the prior alone and independent of the domain. The off-diagonal anisotropy equals the Herfindahl index H of the discarded-mode power exactly, Weyl's eigenvalue counting law fixes the number of discarded modes and hence H, and Berry's random-wave conjecture enters only through a diagonal term D, which we measure directly. Together they predict an approximately flat loss landscape over the penalty exponent, which leaves a learned diagonal regularizer little to gain from tuning the exponent per room. On simulated acoustic rooms the closed form stays within 5.83% of a per-room power-law oracle across observation windows, and three learned diagonal architectures track its error, the closest within a fraction of a point and none more than 3pp above it, while learning qualitatively different spectra. In the truncation regime no tested method consistently improves on the closed form, including Learned Iterative Ridge, which couples modes across layers. The framework extends to heat diffusion through a known Green's-function correction with no new free parameters.

Machine Learning.title: Dream2Discern: Learning from Hard Latent Variants for Runtime Failure Prediction in Multi-Agent Systems
Machine Learning.summary: Reliable deployment of LLM-based multi-agent systems calls for runtime auditors that predict terminal outcomes from observed execution prefixes. These auditors typically learn from a limited corpus of trajectories with verified outcomes. Expanding this corpus requires costly execution and verification, yet broader failure coverage alone provides no explicit criterion for identifying prefixes that the current auditor finds difficult to classify. To this end, we propose Dream2Discern, a runtime auditor trained through implicit augmentation guided by its own prediction loss. During Dream, we select perturbations of the auditor's representation operators to increase prediction loss on recorded prefixes, yielding hard latent variants. During Discern, the auditor learns to predict execution outcomes from these variants using the original labels. The variants are regenerated as the auditor learns, turning a limited corpus into a renewable source of hard examples and requiring no additional trajectory collection or outcome verification. Extensive evaluations on AFTraj-2K and StepShield show that Dream2Discern outperforms competitive failure auditors and achieves over 90% trajectory-level weighted accuracy on both benchmarks while balancing prediction accuracy and timeliness. Project page: https://zbox1005.github.io/dream2discern-project/

Machine Learning.title: Understanding and Reducing Misalignment in Persuasion Optimization
Machine Learning.summary: Frontier models are now trained for complex multi-agent tasks, from running a company to engaging in negotiations. These tasks necessitate training models to be persuasive. But what does this optimization pressure mean for model alignment? In this work, we study how reinforcement learning (RL) training for persuasion affects models' use of misaligned strategies such as evidence fabrication and belief coercion, and what techniques can reduce such misalignment. We find that optimizing sender models solely for receiver belief shifts causes the average number of distinct misaligned strategies used per game to increase by more than 25%, and fabrications per game increase to more than 4 times relative to pre-RL models. We compare various mitigation approaches, including stronger strategy guidance, clean demonstrations, penalizing misaligned strategy usage, and improving the model's ability to detect fabrications. We find that navigating the persuasiveness-misalignment trade-off in this setting is challenging, with the best trade-offs coming from combining guidance on aligned persuasion strategies with reward penalties on misalignment. Overall, our work provides a testbed for assessing misalignment stemming from RL-based persuasion training and shows concrete paths for reducing misalignment. Importantly, it highlights that without direct intervention, persuasion-involved RL environments are likely to naturally lead to large increases in the use of misaligned strategies.

Machine Learning.title: Retrieval-Based In-Context Learning: A Domain Adaptation Framework
Machine Learning.summary: In-context retrieval (ICR) is a retrieval-based form of in-context learning (ICL) in which demonstrations are retrieved from a source database based on similarity to the query, rather than sampled independently. In this work, we formulate ICR as a type of domain adaptation problem, where the source distribution $P$ of the database may differ from the target distribution $Q$ of the test query-label pair. We investigate the performance of ICR under a flexible class of distributional shifts that substantially extends prior work \citep{li2024fine,guo2025retrieval}, and establish theoretical guarantees that quantify the benefits and pitfalls of this learning paradigm. Our theory is verified by experiments on synthetic and language tasks.

Machine Learning.title: NeuroRule: Making Black-Box Neural Networks Explainable through Rule-set Evolution
Machine Learning.summary: High-capacity neural network models have achieved state-of-the-art performance across diverse classification tasks, yet they frequently operate as black-box models, lacking the transparency necessary for critical decision-making. Such opacity creates a persistent trade-off between performance and explainability. This paper proposes a solution to address this gap: the NeuroRule knowledge distillation framework that results in explainable rule-sets from neural network models. NeuroRule adapts the EVOTER rule-set evolution infrastructure to treat neural networks as targets for the evolution process, distilling their performance into concise sets of propositional logic expressions. There are three primary contributions: (1) an evolutionary method for distilling black-box neural network models into explicit rule-set models; (2) a method for making rule sets more explainable by including a conciseness objective to evolution; and (3) a demonstration that the distillation is viable even without access to the original neural network training data. The paper thus establishes that black-box neural network models can be made explainable and therefore useful in real-world applications where trustworthiness is paramount.

Machine Learning.title: Interpretable Graph Partitioning for Spatial Prediction
Machine Learning.summary: Spatial prediction estimates unobserved values from spatially distributed observations. Although flexible predictive models are increasingly available, their practical use remains limited when interpretability is essential. In this study, we formulate a graph partitioning problem to construct a global surrogate model that approximates black-box predictions with simpler representations. Specifically, we select connected subgraphs to minimize within-cluster residuals in vertex-level predictions. Although this formulation can be viewed as a variant of spatial regionalization, it operates on model-based predictions at individual locations rather than predefined areal units. With many locations, this point-level formulation may produce artificial connections between regions, reducing interpretability. We therefore introduce a constraint that excludes such connections while retaining flexible partition boundaries. We theoretically analyze how this constraint affects the resulting partition. We also develop a computational procedure for adjusting partition boundaries. Experimental results show that the proposed method yields spatially coherent partitions with flexible boundaries.

Machine Learning.title: Personal VAD: Speaker-Conditioned Voice Activity Detection
Machine Learning.summary: In this paper, we propose "personal VAD", a system to detect the voice activity of a target speaker at the frame level. This system is useful for gating the inputs to a streaming on-device speech recognition system, such that it only triggers for the target user, which helps reduce the computational cost and battery consumption, especially in scenarios where a keyword detector is unpreferable. We achieve this by training a VAD-alike neural network that is conditioned on the target speaker embedding or the speaker verification score. For each frame, personal VAD outputs the probabilities for three classes: non-speech, target speaker speech, and non-target speaker speech. Under our optimal setup, we are able to train a model with only 130K parameters that outperforms a baseline system where individually trained standard VAD and speaker recognition networks are combined to perform the same task.

Machine Learning.title: How the Classical Baseline Shapes Machine-Learning Speed Claims in Topology Optimization
Machine Learning.summary: Topology optimization places material so that a structure resists deformation under given loads. Machine-learning methods often report large speed-ups over classical, non-learned optimization, but a slow classical code or a less stiff learned design can exaggerate them. We re-ran released code for eight methods on one workstation and studied two in depth: Optimize Any Topology (OAT), a diffusion model that generates designs, and a graph-based neural optimizer. Speeding up only the classical code's finite-element solver cut these two methods' speed-ups by up to 20-fold. We then timed the classical code until its design was at least as stiff as the learned one; for OAT, we read this point off the completed runs. Published timings imply a 134x speed-up for OAT on a 256 x 256 grid; our matched single-design comparisons gave 1.5x to 3.5x. At matched stiffness, the graph-based optimizer was slower than the classical code in all six two-dimensional problems. Of the six other methods, two kept their advantage, one shrank, one reversed and two were not comparable. In an exploratory audit of published claims, language models judged that 8 of 28 speed comparisons in randomly sampled, openly accessible articles lacked evidence of equal design quality; our own review counted 11, so the count depends on who judges. We provide a comparison procedure and a minimum report: classical code, hardware, design quality, what each timing includes, and data-generation and training costs.
Machine Learning.comment: 31 pages, 8 figures, 10 tables. Research article: tests of released code for eight topology-optimization methods and an exploratory audit of published speed claims

Machine Learning.title: Backward Conformal Prediction under Covariate Shift
Machine Learning.summary: Backward conformal prediction (BCP) fixes the size of a prediction set and estimates its miscoverage, but assumes calibration and test data are exchangeable. We extend BCP to covariate shift through importance weighting, preserving its guarantees when the density ratio is known. We show that BCP's tight miscoverage report depends only on the relative weight assigned to missed calibration examples, explaining why a better domain classifier can sometimes produce a worse estimate. Motivated by the fact that BCP depends only on nonconformity scores, we propose estimating density ratios on sorted score vectors rather than high-dimensional inputs. We prove that this approach recovers the same report asymptotically under an interpretable condition and characterize the resulting bias otherwise. Experiments with simulated and benchmark distribution shifts show that the proposed method improves BCP's miscoverage estimates, while score-based weighting consistently yields more accurate estimates than embedding-based weighting.

Machine Learning.title: Autoregressive Decoding as a Martingale: Characterizing the Stochastic Dynamics of LLM Generation
Machine Learning.summary: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable success across a wide range of language tasks. At their core, autoregressive LLMs are conditional probability models that learn to approximate the next-token distribution given the preceding context. Despite this probabilistic nature, the stochastic dynamics of autoregressive decoding have rarely been investigated from a rigorous probabilistic perspective. In this work, we define the per-step prediction error as the difference between the sampled token indicator and the model's conditional predictive distribution, and prove that the cumulative error process is a martingale with respect to the decoding filtration, implying that its conditional first-order moment is identically zero. Beyond this first-order property, we derive a closed-form expression for the second-order behavior of the martingale sequence: its predictable quadratic variation reduces to $\sum_t\left(1-p(y_t\mid y_{<t})\right)$, computable from realized token probabilities alone. This identity establishes a direct theoretical connection between sequence fluctuations and predictive uncertainty during autoregressive decoding. White-box experiments on Llama-3.x and Qwen2.5 families (1B to 72B parameters) verify that the empirically measured second-order moments closely match the theoretical predictions derived from our martingale analysis. These results provide a probabilistic framework for analyzing autoregressive LLM decoding, reveal intrinsic probabilistic fingerprints of different language models, and establish a rigorous mathematical foundation for LLM-generated text detection and uncertainty quantification.

Machine Learning.title: KV-Skill: Forging Expertise in the Model's Native Language
Machine Learning.summary: Task knowledge is commonly stored either as text in the prompt or as an update to model weights. Text is modular but must be interpreted on every use, while weight adaptation makes the resulting capability difficult to load, remove, or share independently. We introduce KV-Skill, a design space of external factorized operators that a frozen language model reads through a lightweight interface. KV-Skill supports two complementary paths. Registration converts an authored text skill into a text-derived operator and trains a shared per-backbone interface. Reward learning develops a compact latent operator directly from task outcomes, with or without an authored skill. Neither path adds positions to the prompt. Across ten benchmarks and four backbones from three model families, converting text to a KV-Skill consistently makes the same procedural knowledge more effective on mathematical reasoning and retrieval tasks. On Qwen3.5-4B LiveMath, registration reaches 77.2 accuracy, compared with 52.0 for the same skill as text (SkillOpt) and 64.5 for SoftSkill. Under matched reward training and parameter budgets, KV-Skill gives the best result in seven of eight matched settings against soft prefixes, prefix tuning, and LoRA. A post-hoc rank analysis further shows that text-derived operators retain nearly all of their benefit with one task-aligned direction per injection layer, while matched random directions fail. Finally, a single shared interface serves eleven diverse skills at once with no loss in average accuracy. These results show that task knowledge can be acquired from text or experience, compressed into an external operator, and deployed separately from the backbone. Code is available at: https://github.com/shawnzhg/KV-Skill
Machine Learning.comment: 17 pages, 4 figures, 18 tables. Zhaowei Han and Xiang Zhang contributed equally to this work. Code: https://github.com/shawnzhg/KV-Skill

Machine Learning.title: CLNO: Conservative Local Neural Operator for Compressible Flow Prediction
Machine Learning.summary: We propose a conservative local neural operator (CLNO) for accurate and generalizable autoregressive prediction of compressible flows. Building upon the locality and translation invariance of the local neural operator (LNO), CLNO introduces a conservative evolution framework based on local subdomains of fixed physical size, separating local mean-state evolution from fine-scale reconstruction. The flow is encoded into subdomain-integrated conservative states and fine-scale features, while a shared local network predicts interface fluxes for finite-volume updates that enforce discrete conservation. A convolutional reconstruction network recovers fine-scale structures using zero-mean basis functions, preserving the updated local means and providing information for subsequent evolution. To accommodate different physical parameters, Reynolds--Mach number conditioning modulates the encoding, flux-prediction, and reconstruction networks, enabling a single model to learn parameter-dependent dynamics and generalize to unseen parameter combinations without retraining. CLNO supports prediction across spatial resolutions, computational domain sizes, and boundary conditions. Numerical experiments demonstrate improved generalization and competitive or higher accuracy compared with LNO, including order-of-magnitude error reductions in representative cases, at approximately three to five times the inference cost on periodic benchmarks. These results demonstrate accurate, generalizable, and physically consistent flow prediction through conservative local evolution and fine-scale reconstruction.

Machine Learning.title: Multi-Marginal Inverse Optimal Transport for Contrastive Learning Via Explicit Anchor-Positive-Negative Coupling
Machine Learning.summary: Inverse Optimal Transport (OT) based methods for representation learning learn representations such that the global OT coupling between a pair of data marginals in the representation space, concentrates on the positive pairs. This is in contrast to previous methods that primarily focused on pairwise matching. However, these methods $\textit{DO NOT}$ utilize negative pairs and hence are not truly contrastive in their approach. We show that this leads to issues of dimensional collapse and hence degraded downstream performance. To alleviate this, we develop a novel multi-marginal (MM) inverse OT (IOT) contrastive learning (CL) approach called Neg-MMIOT-CL, which learns representations such that the global multi-marginal OT (MMOT) coupling between a triple of data marginals, with respect to a carefully designed ground-cost between triplets of data points in the representation space, concentrates on the anchor-positive-negative $\textit{triplets}$. For a latent class model, we empirically show that Neg-MMIOT-CL alleviates dimensional collapse. Furthermore, for a specific choice of ground cost for all triplets in representation space, we prove that the optimal representation configuration for Neg-MMIOT-CL exhibits equiangular property for within-class and across-class representations, which translates to Neural-Collapse when the representation dimension is larger than the number of classes minus one -- a result that is $\textit{previously established only}$ for pairwise contrastive learning methods. Finally, we propose Neg-IOT-CL-PushPull, that is a computationally efficient alternative to Neg-MMIOT-CL, alleviating the high cost of computing MMOT plans needed during implementation. We apply these methods on both synthetic and real-world datasets and show significant improvements over existing OT-based contrastive learning methods.

Machine Learning.title: CHAIN: Calibrated LLM Forecasting via Causal-Temporal Hypergraph Inference
Machine Learning.summary: Large language models have achieved significant progress in event forecasting, yet their probability outputs exhibit systematic calibration bias that varies heterogeneously across different domains and question types, undermining the trustworthiness of probabilistic outputs for decision-making under uncertainty. However, existing calibration methods typically correct probability outputs after prediction is complete, without modeling the structural sources of bias within the prediction process itself. To address this challenge, we decompose probabilistic prediction over causal-temporal hypergraphs into three stages, evidence weighting, evidence aggregation, and source fusion, and propose CHAIN, which designs stage-specific mechanisms to mitigate bias at each stage: (i) modulating the temporal decay function by causal topological distance, (ii) aggregating approximately independent causal chains via Noisy-OR after direction-aware deduplication, and (iii) driving adaptive fusion by causal coverage and directional balance. Experimental results on cross-domain forecasting benchmarks show CHAIN outperforms existing methods in expected calibration error, Brier score, and accuracy. Our project is available at https://github.com/QwenQKing/Chain.

Machine Learning.title: Control Consistency Losses for Diffusion Bridges
Machine Learning.summary: Simulating the conditioned dynamics of diffusion processes, given their initial and terminal states, is an important but challenging problem in the sciences. The difficulty is particularly pronounced for rare events, for which the unconditioned dynamics rarely reach the terminal state. In this work, we propose a novel approach for learning diffusion bridges based on a self-consistency property of the optimal control. The resulting algorithm learns the conditioned dynamics in an iterative online manner, and exhibits strong performance in a range of empirical settings without requiring differentiation through simulated trajectories. Beyond the diffusion bridge setting, we draw connections between our self-consistency framework and recent advances in the wider stochastic optimal control literature.

Machine Learning.title: Inverse Learning of Latent Risk-Neutral Densities from Irregular Option Quotes
Machine Learning.summary: Accurate option prices do not imply accurate recovery of the latent risk-neutral density. We study this distinction with two complementary benchmarks. A controlled benchmark exposes simulator-truth densities for latent evaluation, while a chronological NIFTY benchmark tests only held-out market prices. A two-component lognormal mixture has the lowest aggregate price, $L^1$, Wasserstein, and fixed-tail errors on the synthetic benchmark. Learned operators retain narrower strengths: DeepONet reduces 1% quantile and variance error by 39.0% and 34.6% relative to the mixture, and a quote transformer reduces $L^1$ by 16.4% on the structurally misspecified Merton family. A numerical conditioning analysis explains why these rankings can differ: after enforcing mass and forward constraints, 95 of 126 pricing directions are numerically null, and two densities separated by $L^1 = 0.061$ produce identical prices on the covered strikes. On 524 held-out NIFTY calls, validation-selected test-time adaptation reduces DeepONet RMSE by 28.3%, but per-expiry mixture and SVI fits remain much more accurate. The evidence supports target-dependent inductive bias, not a universal winner.
Machine Learning.comment: 8 pages, 4 figures, 2 tables. Accepted to the 7th ACM International Conference on AI in Finance (ICAIF 2026)

Machine Learning.title: A Nonlinear Time-Series Theory for Constant-step SGD with Momentum
Machine Learning.summary: Constant-step stochastic gradient descent with momentum (SGDM) augments the parameter recursion with a momentum state that carries geometrically decaying memory of past stochastic gradients. We study this coupled recursion as a nonlinear time series and develop a framework for its stationary behavior and distributional limits. The joint parameter-momentum process forgets its initialization geometrically under a finite $p$th moment for $p > 1$, yielding a unique stationary causal solution. Under a second-moment condition, this contraction leads to an invariance principle and quenched Gaussian limit for averaged SGDM, while a small-learning-rate analysis gives a Gaussian limit for the last iterate. In a stochastic-curvature quadratic model, we further study how the rate of initialization forgetting relates to stationary variance and averaged fluctuations.

Machine Learning.title: NAVIR: Neuromorphic Audio-Visual Speech Recognition for Robust Human-Robot Interaction on Edge Hardware
Machine Learning.summary: Voice-controlled interaction in industrial settings is hampered by acoustic noise, which severely degrades audio-only speech recognition. Audio-visual speech recognition (AVSR) addresses this by fusing lip-motion cues with the audio stream, but state-of-the-art pipelines rely on three-dimensional convolutions, recurrent units, and attention modules that exceed the budget of typical edge devices. We present NAVIR, an end-to-end AVSR system targeting the BrainChip Akida neuromorphic processor, which natively supports only sequential two-dimensional convolutional inference. The pipeline factorises spatial and temporal encoding into separate AkidaNet-based modules: a per-frame visual encoder, a temporal video encoder, and a spectrogram audio encoder, fused by a lightweight predictor head and decoded by constrained beam search. Models are trained with connectionist temporal classification on noise-augmented audio and then fine-tuned with quantization-aware training. On the GRID benchmark, the quantized audio-visual model reaches 14.0% word error rate (WER) under noise on the unseen-speaker split and 3.3% WER on the overlapped-speaker split, against 22.5% and 11.8% for audio-only baselines, and it attains 98.6% command accuracy at 1.5% WER on a task-specific industrial-command corpus. Operation-count analysis indicates a 13-fold energy advantage of the spiking formulation over its artificial neural network counterpart at 27.6% mean firing rate. On-board measurements show roughly 5-fold lower energy per inference than a Raspberry Pi central processing unit on the lip-reading model, and over 100-fold lower than a laptop graphics processing unit, while sustaining 14.5 inferences per second. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first complete multimodal AVSR pipeline running on neuromorphic hardware of this class.
Machine Learning.comment: This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication. Copyright may be transferred without notice, after which this version may no longer be accessible

Machine Learning.title: Limit Theory for Online Expectile Estimation under Short and Long Range Dependence
Machine Learning.summary: Expectiles are tail-sensitive distributional summaries with important applications in financial risk measurement and forecasting, yet statistical theory for their online estimation from dependent data remains limited. We study a one-pass, stochastic-gradient algorithm with constant learning rate $γ$ for estimating the marginal expectile of a stationary causal process. The recursion admits a unique stationary causal solution and geometrically forgets its initialization. Under short-range dependence, its last iterate is asymptotically Gaussian at the $\sqrtγ$ scale, with variance governed by the population curvature and the long-run variance of the expectile score. For long-memory linear processes the scale changes to $γ^{β-1/2}\ell(1/γ)$, with a Gaussian limit arising from a fractional Brownian motion integral. We further derive the joint long-memory limit for multiple expectile levels and characterize its limiting covariance structure. Various numerical experiments corroborate the predicted Gaussian approximations and regime-specific fluctuation scales.

Machine Learning.title: When Does Compensating Inherited Quantization Error Help? Mean-Square Guarantees for Layer-Wise Quantization and Their Limits
Machine Learning.summary: Layer-wise post-training quantization methods let each layer compensate for the quantization error inherited from earlier layers. We ask under what assumptions such compensation guarantees a network output error no larger than without it. For linear networks of any depth, with the required calibration Gram matrices invertible, if the rounding error of each layer has zero conditional mean and a deterministic second-moment map common to both schemes, as under subtractive dither on an unbounded grid, then compensation with strengths in $[0,1]$ fixed in advance gives a mean-square output error no larger than no compensation, each scheme being followed along its own trajectory. The exact gain separates error removed directly from reduced excitation of later rounding noise. Outside this setting the comparison can fail. With rectified linear activations it fails for two independent reasons: noise changes activation states, and, even when no state changes, the correction moves error from samples on which a unit is inactive to samples on which it is active. With stable activations, commutators between the calibration projection and the activation patterns bound the excess. With a bounded codebook, even unique exact layer-wise minimizers with no overload can give a larger output error. For fixed rounding errors it already fails for two scalar linear layers, refuting a published universal guarantee. An exact residual identity gives the necessary and sufficient condition on a common layer input. All these comparisons hold the calibration input fixed. On two 8B models at 4 bits, fixed half-strength compensation beat uncompensated rounding in every model, text and draw tested, yet no rule for choosing the strength beat a layer-wise rule consistently, and lowering the full-network loss on the data used to choose did not reliably lower it on new text.

Machine Learning.title: Mode Collapse of Mean-Field Variational Inference
Machine Learning.summary: Mean-field variational inference (MFVI) is a widely used method for approximating high-dimensional probability distributions by product measures. It has been empirically observed that MFVI optimizers often suffer from \emph{mode collapse}. For example, when the target measure $π$ is a mixture $π= w P_0 + (1 - w) P_1$, the MFVI optimizer tends to place most of its mass near a single component of the mixture. This work provides the first \emph{theoretical} explanation of mode collapse in MFVI. Starting from two-component mixtures, we introduce the notion of \emph{$\varepsilon$-separateness} to quantify the separation of the mixture components. We derive explicit bounds on the mass that any MFVI optimizer assigns to each component, when $P_0$ and $P_1$ are $\varepsilon$-separated for sufficiently small $\varepsilon$. We further extend this analysis to mixture target distributions with multiple components. Our results reveal that the occurrence of mode collapse crucially depends on the relative position of the components. To address this issue, we propose \emph{rotational variational inference (RoVI)}, which augments MFVI with a rotation matrix. The numerical studies support our theoretical findings and illustrate improved mode coverage with RoVI in Bayesian mixture posteriors, including a real-data example.

Machine Learning.title: Certified but Private: Scalable Zero-Knowledge Proofs for Neural Network Guarantees
Machine Learning.summary: With the growing deployment of machine learning models, formal guarantees of the robustness and fairness of these models have become increasingly important in safety-critical and legal-compliance settings. However, model parameters are often commercial secrets that cannot be disclosed to auditors or end users. To this end, we present PANDA, a scalable system that uses zero-knowledge proofs (ZKPs) to prove the robustness and fairness properties of a model without revealing its private parameters. PANDA is built on top of CROWN, an efficient robustness certification framework that is used in many state-of-the-art formal verification tools for neural networks. The core contribution of PANDA is a novel algorithm for proving linear relaxation bounds for non-linear activation layers, yielding simple, lightweight proofs. Remarkably, our system can generate proofs of local robustness for neural networks with more than 2.9M parameters in 5 minutes, and can verify them in 10 seconds. Prior ZKP-based robustness system rely on exponential-time algorithms that cannot scale to nontrivial networks. In contrast, PANDA scales polynomially in the number of neurons in a network, allowing us to support neural networks 4 orders of magnitude larger than previous approaches with significantly reduced prover overhead.
Machine Learning.comment: 23 pages, 2 figures (11 pages for the main text), accepted to NeurIPS 2026, for code of implementation and evaluation, see https://github.com/youweizhong/PANDA

Machine Learning.title: Real vs. Complex Spectral Bases for Neural Operators: The Role of Green's Function Alignment
Machine Learning.summary: Fourier Neural Operators (FNO) learn solution operators of partial differential equations by parameterizing global convolutions in the complex Fourier domain. For real-valued PDE solutions, the complex FFT carries representational redundancy through conjugate symmetry. We introduce the Hartley Neural Operator (HNO), the exact real-valued mirror of FNO: it replaces the FFT with the purely real Discrete Hartley Transform and learns a single real multiplier per retained spectral mode, with no complex arithmetic. Because the real Hartley spectrum is not halved by conjugate symmetry, HNO retains twice as many frequency corners as FNO but one real weight where FNO carries a complex pair, so the two operators are iso-parametric at equal width and differ only in spectral basis. Our central thesis is that the best basis is a property of the operator. Self-adjoint elliptic operators (Poisson, biharmonic) have real, symmetric Green's functions that the real Hartley multiplier diagonalizes exactly, and HNO is favored there. Time-dependent operators carry phase, from oscillation in the wave equation to transport in advection, Burgers, and Navier-Stokes, which a real diagonal multiplier cannot represent, so FNO is favored there, and increasingly so with the operator's phase content, leaving the phaseless heat equation as the borderline case. Training both operators identically and benchmarking across PDE classes, initial-condition families, and boundary conditions, we find an elliptic-versus-time-dependent split that is monotone in operator phase content and matches the Green's-function theory we develop. Rather than a universal winner, our findings give a predictive rule: match the spectral basis to the symmetry of the solution operator.
Machine Learning.comment: Extended version of the paper accepted at the 62nd Allerton Conference on Communication, Control, and Computing (2026)

Machine Learning.title: Certified Robustness via Sparse Second-Order Cone Relaxations
Machine Learning.summary: Certified robustness is critical for deploying neural networks in safety-sensitive settings, but computing exact certificates typically requires solving nonconvex optimization problems. Practical verifiers use convex relaxations: linear programming (LP) relaxations are scalable but often too conservative, whereas semidefinite programming (SDP) relaxations can be substantially tighter but are computationally expensive. We introduce a hierarchy of second-order cone programming (SOCP) relaxations that provide stronger certificates than LP while avoiding the cost of global positive-semidefinite constraints. Our construction combines convex-hull relaxations of ReLU activations, selective McCormick lifting over certified variable bounds, and second-order cone constraints induced by 2-by-2 principal minors. Adding these constraints progressively yields a monotone hierarchy of increasingly tight bounds with a controllable computation-tightness trade-off. On fully connected and convolutional networks on MNIST and CIFAR-10, SOCP-based verification improves certified robust accuracy over LP-based verification and is competitive with alpha,beta-CROWN, while remaining orders of magnitude faster than SDP-based verification. These results position selective second-order constraints as a practical middle ground between scalable LP-based and tight SDP-based certification. Finally, we introduce class-optimized robust evaluation (CORE), which applies tighter relaxations only to target classes not certified by cheaper ones. On the fully connected MNIST benchmark, CORE variants match SDP-cert's certified robust accuracy while reducing average verification time by up to 86.30%.

Machine Learning.title: Poisson-GENERIC Neural Operators: Exact Metriplectic Structure in Function Space via Casimir Entropies
Machine Learning.summary: Existing thermodynamically consistent neural operators enforce GENERIC degeneracy by projecting the reversible operator, introducing state dependence without guaranteeing Jacobi. We instead use a compatible Lie--Poisson pencil $L=αD+λ(uD+Du)$ for nonlinear transport and constant Poisson multipliers otherwise. Augmenting the observed field $u$ with latent entropy density $s$ makes $S=\int s$ a Casimir, so $L\,δS/δz=0$ without projection. Energy combines a fixed mechanical quadratic, learned gauge-free potential, and convex internal energy. The friction operator $M=AA^\top$ enforces $M\,δE/δz=0$ pointwise and supports diffusion and damping without an independent reversible transport generator. Skewness, positivity, and both degeneracies hold exactly; the continuum pencil satisfies Jacobi, verified numerically on the alias-free band. The parameterization represents the closed-form heat and damped-wave friction operators within its admissible range. Physical energy is bounded under coercivity assumptions, while a discrete-gradient integrator preserves both laws when solved to convergence. Across four PDEs in 1D and 2D and three backbones (FNO, Transolver, CNO), the model wins 61/72 seed-level comparisons against matched unconstrained baselines, recovers exact transport and wave symbols, matches heat and Burgers dissipation within 13%, and exhibits negligible advection dissipation. A constant-$L$ ablation exposes the cost of nonlinear transport, while a learned-energy ablation shows that conserving learned energy need not constrain physical energy.

Machine Learning.title: GENERIC-FNO: Embedding Energy Conservation and Entropy Production into Fourier Neural Operators
Machine Learning.summary: We propose GENERIC-FNO, a neural operator that embeds the metriplectic (GENERIC) degeneracy structure of nonequilibrium thermodynamics in function space, coupling reversible, energy-conserving dynamics to irreversible, entropy-producing dynamics via the degeneracy conditions. Prior structure-preserving neural operators enforce at most one conservation law or a Hamiltonian form, and thermodynamically consistent learning has been confined to finite-dimensional, graph, or particle systems. GENERIC-FNO learns the energy and entropy functionals as neural operators and builds the reversible and irreversible operators as diagonal Fourier multipliers flanked by rank-one projections that enforce both degeneracy conditions exactly, by construction, with no penalty, update projection, or residual; the Jacobi identity is not enforced. The identities hold to machine precision (~10^-13) for any initialization, dimension, or resolution, so the continuous-time dynamics conserve the learned energy and produce the learned entropy exactly, with explicit time stepping adding only an O(dt^2) drift. These are guarantees about the learned functionals within GENERIC's scope of closed conservative-dissipative dynamics, not a certificate of physical accuracy, and the (E,S,L,M) decomposition is not unique; we make this gauge freedom explicit and propose a gauge-invariant dissipation diagnostic independent of the learned functionals. Across three backbones (1D/2D FNO, DeepONet) and four canonical scalar PDEs, the guarantees transfer zero-shot over a 4x super-resolution range and hold in 3D; the diagnostic identifies the reversible and the most dissipative system in every backbone; and over 200-step rollouts, where every unconstrained model we test diverges or collapses, GENERIC-FNO stays bounded, at half the parameters but 4-10x the compute, while losing accuracy on pure transport and on the smallest 1D backbone.

Machine Learning.title: Improving the Evaluation of Biomedical Question Answering with Few Human Preference Signals
Machine Learning.summary: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems are increasingly used for biomedical Question Answering (QA). However, evaluating their effectiveness remains challenging due to the lack of reliable reference resources and the frequent misalignment between automatic evaluation metrics and human judgments. One practical question is how evaluation results should be used to guide development decisions, especially when they correlate weakly with human judgments and may even lead to different conclusions. We explore how to use a small amount of human preference signals to calibrate direct assessment evaluation metrics, and show that calibrated metrics consistently outperform baselines that either treat all metrics equally or rely on a single best metric across multiple datasets.

Machine Learning.title: Single-Loop Stochastic Projected Damped Extragradient Methods for Nonconvex--(Strongly) Concave Minimax Optimization
Machine Learning.summary: We develop single-loop stochastic projected damped extragradient methods for nonconvex--(strongly) concave minimax optimization, with complexity guarantees for both game stationarity (GS) and optimization stationarity (OS). Our approach combines a stochastic projected damped extragradient (SPDE) method with a recursive variance-reduced variant, VR-SPDE, both of which retain a single-loop structure. Under an unbiased stochastic gradient oracle with uniformly bounded variance, SPDE finds an $\varepsilon$-game-stationary point with stochastic first-order oracle (SFO) complexities of $O(κ\varepsilon^{-4})$ and $O(\varepsilon^{-5})$ in the nonconvex--strongly concave and nonconvex--concave settings, respectively, where $κ=L/μ$. Under an additional mean-square Lipschitz condition on the stochastic gradients, VR-SPDE improves these GS complexities to $O(κ^{3/2}\varepsilon^{-3})$ and $O(\varepsilon^{-9/2})$, respectively. For an $\varepsilon$-optimization-stationary point, SPDE achieves SFO complexities of $O(κ\varepsilon^{-4})$ and $O(\varepsilon^{-6})$, while VR-SPDE achieves $O(κ^{3/2}\varepsilon^{-3})$ and $O(\varepsilon^{-6})$, in the two settings, respectively. These OS guarantees match the best-known bounds achieved by multi-loop methods while preserving a single-loop implementation. To the best of our knowledge, our results provide the best-known SFO complexity guarantees among single-loop stochastic first-order methods for the respective stationarity criteria and problem classes.

Machine Learning.title: A 4-Qubit Variational Quantum Classifier for Sequence-Specific Classification of DNMT3A and DNMT3B Flanking Methylation Preferences
Machine Learning.summary: DNA methylation is a critical epigenetic modification that regulates gene expression and genome stability, primarily catalyzed by the DNA methyltransferase 3 (DNMT3) family of enzymes. Distinguishing precise sequence-specific flanking preferences between DNMT3A and DNMT3B remains computationally challenging due to the complex and high-dimensional nature of biochemical sequence data. In this study, we propose a novel Quantum Machine Learning (QML) approach to classify DNA methylation preferences, leveraging a Variational Quantum Classifier (VQC). Using experimentally derived deep enzymology data, we constructed a dataset containing 4,096 unique NNNCGNNN motifs. We evaluated a four-qubit VQC using a custom NumPy exact-statevector simulator. The described two-layer circuit contains 24 trainable rotations, eight CNOT gates, and eight input-encoding rotations, totaling 40 gates before measurement. Across five initialization seeds, the revised VQC evaluation achieved a ROC-AUC of 0.661 pm 0.009, where variability denotes sample standard deviation. The held-out test partition is approximately balanced, containing 200 DNMT3A-labeled motifs and 210 DNMT3B-labeled motifs. An always-DNMT3B predictor achieves 51.2% accuracy and a balanced accuracy of 0.500 on this test partition. This proof-of-concept establishes a foundation for utilizing near-term quantum architectures in complex epigenetic classification tasks, paving the way for hybrid quantum-classical pipelines in bioinformatics.
Machine Learning.comment: Accepted at IEEE International Conference on Quantum Artificial Intelligence (QAI) 2026

Machine Learning.title: TorchSpin: Differentiable Electron Paramagnetic Resonance Simulation in PyTorch
Machine Learning.summary: Interpreting electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) spectra commonly requires repeated forward simulation and optimization of spin Hamiltonian parameters. Established software provides mature simulation and fitting methods, but these calculations are not generally available as differentiable components within machine-learning workflows. We present TorchSpin, an open-source PyTorch framework that ports the organization and numerical conventions of EasySpin into a tensor-based computational environment. Representative calculations spanning continuous-wave EPR, ENDOR, pulse EPR, spin dynamics, trajectory simulation, and magnetometry closely reproduced corresponding EasySpin results. In matched benchmarks, TorchSpin CPU execution was faster than EasySpin for six of nine workloads although performance depended strongly on the calculation. We therefore focused on the capabilities enabled by automatic differentiation in PyTorch. In a Cu(II) powder-spectrum demonstration, feedback propagated through TorchSpin improved the quality of a supervised convolutional neural network (CNN) without using parameter labels during refinement. Models trained from randomly initialized CNNs using only noisy spectra and TorchSpin reconstruction loss achieved median similarities of $\geq$ 0.99. CNNs trained on TorchSpin-generated libraries also transferred without adaptation to independently generated EasySpin spectra with performance comparable to EasySpin-trained controls. Once trained, the CNN produced initial parameter estimates in approximately 1 ms per spectrum while a batch of 512 was processed in approximately 1.3 ms with GPU acceleration. TorchSpin therefore provides both a tested Python implementation of established EPR calculations and a differentiable physical layer for rapid learned inference, spectral refinement, and parameter-label-free training.

Machine Learning.title: Interpolation of GEDI Biomass Estimates with Calibrated Uncertainty Quantification
Machine Learning.summary: Wall-to-wall biomass density estimation from NASA's GEDI mission requires interpolating sparse LIDAR observations across heterogeneous landscapes. While Random Forest and XGBoost are widely used, they predict each location independently from satellite features, without adapting to the varying difficulty of heterogeneous landscapes. We introduce Attentive Neural Processes (ANPs), a probabilistic meta-learning architecture that explicitly conditions predictions on local observation sets as well as geospatial foundation model embeddings. ANPs learn a flexible spatial covariance approximator that is more uncertain in complex landscapes and less in homogeneous areas. We validate this approach across five distinct biomes ranging from tropical Amazonian forests to boreal, temperate, and alpine ecosystems, demonstrating that ANPs achieve competitive accuracy while maintaining uncertainty calibration. We demonstrate a scalable, empirically calibrated alternative to ensemble architectures for continental-scale biomass mapping.

Machine Learning.title: Popularity Trajectories and Mixing Patterns of Urban Venues in Two European Cities
Machine Learning.summary: Urban venues such as restaurants, shops, bars and parks host the daily life of a city, and their collective rise and fall signals how vibrant a neighbourhood is. The usual assumption is that a venue's fortunes follow its neighbourhood's, so that how wealthy an area is and how many people live there will decide a venue's performance. Yet whether there is a common performance trajectory shared by venues over time is underexplored. In this study, we use 5.5 years of Foursquare data for about 10^4 venues in London and Barcelona. We found six distinguishable shapes recur in both cities, that are (1) Fall, (2) Rise, (3) Rise & Fall, (4) Steady, (5) Ephemeral (an early hit that loses popularity fast) and (6) Underdogs (a slow starter that gains popularity late). However, no recovery shape appears, that is neither city yields a U-shaped fall-and-rise group. Additionally, we found that deprivation and population density are not indicative which shape a venue follows. We also discovered that how early a shape can be recognized depends on when its distinctive segment occurs, not a shape's complexity. Proximity between venues, however, does predict how well-performing a venue is. We uncovered a mixing pattern where venues of the same shape tend to locate together more often than chance within roughly 200 to 600 metres. Finally, our qualitative reading of two contrasting districts, one rising in London and one falling in Barcelona, show that comparable socioeconomic conditions but divergent gentrification histories can generate vastly different popularity trajectories. All in all, our results altogether point at that urban vibrancy emerges at the block- and street- level, and social and historical contexts matter in terms of the characteristics of such patterns.
Machine Learning.comment: 18 pages for main body, 8 pages for supplementary materials; 5 figures and 2 tables in main body, 7 figures and 9 tables in supplementary materials

Human-Computer Interaction.title: The Dynamics of Delusion: Modeling Bidirectional False Belief Amplification in Human-Chatbot Dialogue
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: There is growing concern that AI chatbots might fuel delusional beliefs in users. Some have suggested that humans and chatbots mutually reinforce false beliefs over time, but quantitative evidence is lacking. Using a unique dataset of chat logs from individuals who exhibited delusional thinking, we developed a latent state model that captures accumulating and decaying influences between humans and chatbots. We find that a bidirectional influence model substantially outperforms a unidirectional alternative where humans are the primary driver of delusion. We find that humans exert strong but short-lived influence on chatbots, whereas chatbots exert longer-lasting influence on humans. Moreover, chatbots exert strong, stable self-influence over their own future outputs that tends to perpetuate delusions over long stretches of conversation. In fact, this chatbot self-influence constituted the dominant pathway when considering accumulated influence over time. Overall, these results indicate that humans tend to drive sharp, immediate increases in delusion, whereas chatbots sustain and propagate these effects over longer timescales. Together, these findings provide the first empirical, quantitative evidence that human-chatbot interactions can form feedback loops of delusion, decomposable into distinct pathways with dissociable temporal dynamics. By doing so, they can inform the development of safer AI systems.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Agency as a New Organizing Abstraction for Computer Science
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Advances in large-scale machine learning have enabled agentic AI systems: persistent, autonomous computational entities that pursue goals, initiate actions, and interact with open environments. These systems are often framed as applications of foundation models. We argue that this framing is incomplete: agency is also a candidate new organizing abstraction for computer science. What is new is not the concept of an agent, nor runtime policy generation per se, but its general-purpose, open-ended form, in which systems can synthesize courses of action from goals, observations, and memory, over tools and environments for which no complete task-specific model was specified in advance. Thus agency becomes a systems-level abstraction as well as an AI modeling concept. Where the process abstraction organizes computation around executing programs, agency organizes it around pursuing goals under bounded resources: a process executes a program; an agent pursues a goal. From this perspective, the recurring failures of deployed agentic systems (runaway resource consumption, behavior redirected by adversarial content, opaque continuous operation) are symptoms of structural abstraction gaps, not isolated engineering defects. We examine these gaps across six dimensions (execution, interfaces, correctness, oversight, coordination, and persistence) and argue that closing them requires coordinated advances in systems,
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: An extended version of a paper to appear in Communications of the ACM, November 2026

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Get In, Decide, Prove: A Merchant-Side Readiness Benchmark for Agentic Commerce
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: AI agents now browse and buy on people's behalf, and benchmarks measure how well the agents perform. Far less is known about the other side of the transaction: whether a merchant's website lets an agent in, publishes terms precise enough to decide a purchase, and leaves evidence of what was agreed. This paper presents a merchant-side benchmark built on those three questions and reports a pilot of it. The central measurement, decision sufficiency, rates each criterion of a concrete buyer mandate (total cost, cancellation or return terms, service date, variant identity) as determinate, indeterminate, or unknown from the merchant's own published evidence. Readiness scores carry their evidence coverage and missingness bounds; access is reported separately for a declared bot, a declared headless browser, and a user-present browser; and each observed term is mapped to the RAILS admissibility class of the evidence that could support it in a dispute. Four large merchants received the full assessment: three refused the declared profiles at their offer pages, and no mandate could be confirmed as met, because each merchant left a total or a refund term undetermined. An access census of 555 sites of merchants that two payment processors publicly name as clients found the home page unreadable to both declared profiles at 105 sites (18.9%). A declared assessment of 330 merchants, scored by deterministic rules without a rater, found that evidence coverage rather than the score decides who can be ranked: 115 merchants (35%) reached the ranking threshold, rankable profiles scored a median of 89 to 90, and material terms was the one pillar well below the others, because the all-in total was decidable at 18 merchants. The pilot shows that the measurements can be taken; it does not validate them or rank merchants, and the weights and the projected clearing band await validation against outcomes.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 23 pages, 7 figures, 10 tables. Companion dataset: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23325184

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Brain2Face: A Study on the Relation of EEG Signals and Spatio-temporal Head Avatars
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Driving digital head avatars is classically done by hand-crafted artist design or by image-based facial performance capture. In this work, we ask whether spatio-temporal tracking of the humans's head geometry and appearance can be performed solely from brain signals, i.e., Electroencephalography (EEG). Since prior work mostly focused on activity and emotion recognition, this task is relatively unexplored without even having publicly available high-quality datasets and benchmarks. Thus, we contribute a dataset featuring paired EEG and human head geometry as well as appearance annotations. We synchronize 64-channel EEG with per-frame expression latent codes of a personalized Gaussian head avatar. Second, we introduce a baseline to the task of expression recovery of a head avatar from EEG signals. To this end, we propose a dedicated EEG-to-expression model that takes a temporal sequence of EEG signals as input and regresses the latent expression parameters of the 3D Gaussian head avatar. Lastly, we validate our capture and algorithmic design choices through a benchmark protocol that we introduce to this task. We believe this work paves the way towards better understanding of the relation between EEG signals and facial surface as well as appearance changes.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: Project page: https://vcai.mpi-inf.mpg.de/projects/Brain2Face

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Human Situational Awareness and Workload during Heterogeneous Autonomous Vehicle Hazard Monitoring: A Cross-Platform Study
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: As autonomous ground and aerial vehicles become increasingly capable, human operators are transitioning from direct control to supervisory monitoring roles. Maintaining Situational Awareness (SA) during rare but safety critical hazard events remains a fundamental challenge, particularly when operators must monitor heterogeneous autonomous platforms with different spatial and cognitive demands. This study develops a unified experimental framework for investigating human SA and workload during supervisory monitoring of autonomous ground and aerial vehicles under hazard conditions. Eighteen participants completed six within-subject conditions combining three interface modalities, namely, visual-only, haptic-only, and visual-haptic, with two platform types, ground vehicle and aerial drone. SA was measured using Situation Awareness Rating Technique (SART), while workload was assessed using the NASA Task Load Index (NASA-TLX). The key findings are: 1) Aerial monitoring produced significantly lower overall SA, higher situational demand, and greater workload than ground monitoring, driven by elevated Demand and reduced Understanding rather than diminished Supply. 2) Workload was consistently coupled with situational demand across all conditions, suggesting a stable SA-workload mechanism. 3) Both haptic-only and visual-haptic significantly improved overall SA relative to visual-only without increasing workload, demonstrating that interface design can enhance awareness within the existing workload envelope. These findings establish a cross-platform behavioural baseline for designing multimodal interfaces that enhance operator SA without elevating workload in heterogeneous autonomous vehicle systems.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Calibrating LLM Explanations to Human Decisions with Reinforcement Learning
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Explanations of LLM outputs are considered an important way to make model behavior legible, helping human users make good decisions on downstream tasks. However, default training approaches for improving explanations target model task performance or human preference rather than human decision quality. To bridge this gap, we introduce \textbf{HD-RL}, a reinforcement learning framework for optimizing LLM explanations for human decision making. Our approach calibrates a human decision simulator on observed human decisions, applying a proxy reward model to optimize the LLM to generate explanations that help people to make good decisions. We apply this framework to AI-generated text detection. In our initial data collection phase, we observed that while LLMs possess strong autonomous detection capabilities, the explanations they generate for users yield near-random human accuracy (51.3\%). By applying the HD-RL framework to the open-source Qwen 3.6 model, we generate optimized explanations that improve human performance, achieving a GLMM-estimated human accuracy of 63.7\% in a randomized between-subjects experiment with repeated measures and outperforming RLVR, RLAIF, and other baselines by over 8\%.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: TouchTwin: Human-AI Haptic Authoring for 3D-Scanned Tabletop Scenes through Language and Touch
